A referral that [AGENCY NAME] declined or could not serve, with the reason recorded.
A specific, assigned and dated step taken in response to an evaluation finding.

procedures: The governing body sets an annual evaluation calendar. The evaluation covers the prior calendar year and is completed and signed by March 31 each year.

By January 31, the Agency Director assigns the evaluators, who include the Agency Director, the Service Supervisor and at least one governing body member. The names and roles are recorded in the report.

The scheduler and Agency Director compile data for the year: number of clients served (active, new, closed), total hours or units of service by payer (Medicaid PCS, CAP/DA, private pay), and service types.
The Agency Director compiles the number of referrals not accepted and the reasons (for example staffing, outside the service area, needs beyond scope), from the CLN-04 intake log.

The Agency Director compiles the number of discharges and discontinuations by reason (goals met, client request, hospitalization, death, nonpayment, safety, loss of Medicaid authorization) from the CLN-10 records.
The Service Supervisor summarizes client outcomes using plan-of-care reviews, supervisory visit reports and changes in condition, and reports on whether plan-of-care goals were met.
The Agency Director evaluates staffing adequacy: aide-to-client capacity, missed or late visits (CLN-19), turnover, RN coverage hours (ADM-06) and training and competency compliance (PER-02, PER-05).

The evaluators review complaints and grievances (CLN-02), incidents (CLN-15), abuse, neglect and exploitation reports and HCPR referrals (CLN-14, CLN-11), exposure events (ADM-14) and DHSR inspection findings (SUP-02).
The evaluators review the four most recent 90-day record review reports (ADM-09) and note recurring problems.
The evaluators obtain input from clients or representatives (satisfaction survey or telephone interviews) and from aides and office staff, and record the method and the number of responses.
For Medicaid clients, the evaluators review authorization and billing accuracy and EVV capture rates (MED-01, MED-03, ADM-17).
The evaluators write the report with findings and conclusions. Each finding that needs action has a corrective or improvement action, a responsible person and a target date.
The governing body reviews the report at a meeting, adopts it by recorded vote, and the minutes note the actions assigned.
The Agency Director tracks the actions and reports progress at each subsequent governing body meeting. Unfinished actions are carried over to the next evaluation.
The Agency Director revises policies, staffing or training as the findings require, and updates this manual under ADM-16.
The signed evaluation report and supporting data are kept in the administrative file and made available to DHSR on request.

responsibilities.duty: Completes the annual evaluation, adopts the report and ensures corrective actions are carried out.
Organizes the evaluation, compiles data, writes the report and tracks actions.
Provides outcomes, supervisory visit and clinical quality data and takes part in the evaluation.
Provides service hours, non-acceptance and missed-visit data.

documentation: Signed annual program evaluation report listing evaluators, methods, findings and actions
Supporting data (clients served, hours, outcomes, staffing, non-acceptances, discharge reasons)
Client and staff survey results
Governing body minutes adopting the report
Action tracking log with completion dates

policies.title: Client Record Review Every 90 Days
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Agency Director, Service Supervisor and designated record reviewers
policies.purpose: To review a sample of active and closed client records every 90 days to confirm that records are complete, that services follow the plan of care and that problems are found and corrected promptly.
policies.policy:
This policy meets Administrative Policies item .1004(d&e), Client record review policy, 10A NCAC 13J .1004.

At least once every 90 days, [AGENCY NAME] reviews a sample of active client records and a sample of closed client records. The review is carried out under the direction of the governing body. The record of each review names the reviewers, describes the method (how the sample was chosen and the checklist used) and documents the findings and corrective actions.

The review checks, at a minimum, that: the RN's initial in-home assessment was done and signed before the plan of care; the plan of care is signed and current and was reviewed on schedule (CLN-06); supervisory visits were made on time by the RN (CLN-08); signed client rights and responsibilities notices, the service agreement and the complaint procedure with the DHSR hotline are on file (CLN-01, CLN-02, CLN-18); aide visit notes match the plan of care; changes in condition and incidents were reported and acted on; Medicaid authorizations are in place where applicable (MED-01); and closed records have a documented discharge reason and a discharge summary (CLN-10). Results are reported to the governing body, which makes sure corrective actions are completed.

definitions.definition: The record of a client who is currently receiving services.
The record of a client who has been discharged or whose services have been discontinued.
The group of records selected for each 90-day review.

procedures: The Agency Director sets the review dates for the year so that a review is done at least every 90 days. The dates are placed on the compliance calendar.

The Agency Director appoints the reviewers for each cycle. The Service Supervisor takes part, and at least one reviewer who did not provide the care or author the record is included where staffing allows. Reviewer names are recorded.

At each review, the Agency Director pulls a sample that includes both active and closed records. As an agency standard, the sample is the greater of 10% of each group or 5 records from each group (all records if fewer). The sample includes Medicaid and private pay clients and each aide's clients.
The Agency Director records the sampling method on the review form, including the date, the number of active and closed records, and how they were selected.
Reviewers use the standard 90-day record review checklist to check each record for the items listed in the policy section.
Reviewers verify that the plan of care has been reviewed within 90 days or sooner after a change in condition, and that the review is signed and dated by the RN (CLN-06).
Reviewers verify that supervisory visits were done on schedule by the RN and that each visit report is complete (CLN-08).
Reviewers verify that signed rights notices, service agreement and complaint information are present and dated before services began (CLN-01, CLN-02, CLN-18).
Reviewers compare a sample of aide visit notes and timekeeping or EVV records with the plan of care and the schedule to confirm services match (MED-03, CLN-12).
Reviewers check closed records for the documented discharge reason, the notice given to the client and the discharge summary (CLN-10) and for filing and retention compliance (CLN-12).

Reviewers record each deficiency on the review form with the client record number (not the client's name on any report sent outside the agency), the action required, the person responsible and a due date, usually within 14 days.

The Service Supervisor or responsible person corrects the deficiency, signs and dates the correction on the form, and the Agency Director verifies it. Staff-performance concerns are handled under PER-04.

The Agency Director prepares a summary of the review (number reviewed, compliance rate, trends and actions) and presents it to the governing body at its next meeting. The minutes record that it was received.
The Agency Director keeps the review forms and summary in the administrative file. The trends from the four reviews of the year feed into the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).
Review information is handled as confidential protected information (ADM-15).

responsibilities.duty: Directs the 90-day review, receives results and makes sure corrective actions are completed.
Schedules reviews, draws the sample, compiles findings, verifies corrections and reports to the governing body.
Takes part in the review and corrects clinical record deficiencies.
Complete the checklist accurately and keep client information confidential.

documentation: Completed 90-day record review forms with date, reviewers, sampling method and findings
Corrective action log with due dates and completion dates
Summary report to the governing body and the minutes that record it
Compliance calendar showing review dates

policies.title: Infection Control and Communicable Disease Exposure
policies.applies_to: All employees, including in-home aides, the RN/Service Supervisor, scheduler/intake and office staff, and contracted staff
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and staff by setting written infection control and communicable disease practices, identifying employee risk categories and meeting state and OSHA requirements.
policies.policy:
This policy meets Administrative Policies item .1003(a) infection control, Infection control policies with Employee risk categories identified, and item 1003(a), Written policies regarding infection control and exposure to communicable diseases consistent with Subchapter 19A of Title 15A NCAC, including provisions for compliance with 29 CFR 1910 (OSHA), 10A NCAC 13J .1003(a).

[AGENCY NAME] follows written infection control and communicable disease policies that are consistent with 15A NCAC Subchapter 19A and that provide for compliance with the OSHA General Industry Standards at 29 CFR 1910, including the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard at 29 CFR 1910.1030. Related requirements are in ADM-11 (bloodborne pathogens), ADM-12 (TB screening using Form DHHS 3405), ADM-13 (hepatitis B vaccination or declination) and ADM-14 (exposure control plan and post-exposure follow-up).

EMPLOYEE RISK CATEGORIES. Each position is assigned a risk category in its job description. Category I (routine risk): in-home aides and the RN/Service Supervisor when providing or supervising hands-on care, who may have contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, soiled linens, sharps or ill clients. Category I staff must have a baseline TB skin test, be offered hepatitis B vaccination, and receive annual airborne and bloodborne pathogen training under the exposure control plan. Category II (occasional or limited risk): staff who sometimes visit homes but do not provide hands-on care, such as the Agency Director on home visits or a scheduler doing a home safety check. Category II staff follow standard precautions and receive infection control orientation. Category III (no routine risk): office-only staff with no client contact. Category III staff receive general infection control orientation. If a Category II or III employee is assigned hands-on duties, the person is reclassified as Category I and meets all Category I requirements before the first such assignment.

STANDARD PRACTICES. All staff use standard precautions with every client. Hands are washed with soap and water or cleaned with an alcohol-based hand rub before and after client contact, before preparing food, after toileting or handling soiled items, after removing gloves and when visibly soiled. Staff use gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection suited to the task. Sharps are handled as little as possible and put into puncture-resistant containers. Regulated and contaminated waste is handled per the exposure control plan. Soiled linen and clothing are handled with gloves, bagged where used and not shaken. Reusable equipment is cleaned and disinfected with an EPA-registered disinfectant. Aides do not provide care while they have symptoms of a communicable illness (for example fever, vomiting, diarrhea, undiagnosed rash or productive cough). They report to the supervisor and are excluded from client contact until cleared as set out below. When a client has a known or suspected communicable disease, the RN decides on added precautions and records them in the plan of care.

The policy is reviewed at least annually and revised when state or federal requirements change.

definitions.definition: Infection prevention practices applied to all clients regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, PPE, safe sharps handling, respiratory hygiene, safe waste and linen handling, and cleaning of equipment.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.
An employee whose job involves a routine risk of exposure to blood, body fluids or communicable disease.
A specific contact with blood or other potentially infectious material, or with a communicable disease, that results from the performance of an employee's duties.

procedures: The Agency Director assigns a risk category (I, II or III) to each position and records it in the job description (ADM-07) and in the employee's personnel file.

Before first client contact, each Category I employee completes infection control orientation covering this policy, standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use, sharps and waste handling, and exclusion of ill staff (PER-06). Completion is documented.

Hands-on staff receive baseline TB screening per ADM-12, using Form DHHS 3405. Hepatitis B vaccination is offered, or a signed declination is obtained, per ADM-13. Records are kept in the personnel file.

Category I employees receive airborne and bloodborne pathogen training at hire and at least annually, as required under the exposure control plan (ADM-11, ADM-14). Attendance is recorded as in-service education (PER-05).

The Agency Director makes sure that each Category I employee has the supplies needed for the work: gloves in the sizes needed, gowns or aprons, masks, eye protection, alcohol-based hand rub, a small sharps container if needed, disposable bags and an EPA-registered disinfectant. The supervisor replaces supplies within one working day of a request.
Aides wash or sanitize their hands and put on PPE following the procedure taught in orientation, and they remove and dispose of PPE before leaving the home or touching shared surfaces.

Aides place used sharps in a puncture-resistant container, never recap needles and report any sharps found in the home to the RN. Aides do not handle clients' own sharps unless the plan of care and demonstrated competency allow it.
Aides bag contaminated waste and soiled linen as taught, and they clean and disinfect reusable equipment and surfaces that become contaminated.

The RN checks the client's known communicable disease status at assessment (CLN-05). If the client has a known or suspected communicable disease, the RN decides on added precautions, writes them in the plan of care, teaches the aide and documents it.

An aide who has symptoms of a communicable illness calls the supervisor at [PHONE] before the shift. The supervisor decides on exclusion from client contact and a return date, relying on health care provider guidance and 15A NCAC 19A, and arranges replacement coverage under CLN-19.
An aide who is excluded returns to work only when cleared by the RN or Agency Director, with a health care provider's note when the illness requires it. The clearance is documented.

The Service Supervisor notifies the clients who may have been exposed when a communicable disease in an employee could have affected them, in consultation with the local health department, and documents the notice. Reportable conditions are reported to the local health department as 15A NCAC 19A requires.
After any exposure incident, the employee follows ADM-14 immediately, including first aid, reporting to the supervisor and post-exposure evaluation. The incident is recorded under CLN-15.
The Agency Director reviews this policy and the risk category assignments at least annually, revises them as needed, records the review date and retrains staff on any changes (ADM-16).
During the 90-day record review and the annual program evaluation, the Agency Director reviews infection control and exposure events and corrects any trends (ADM-08, ADM-09).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and makes sure resources are available for infection control.
Assigns risk categories, ensures supplies, training, screening and vaccination offers, and reviews the policy annually.
Assesses clients for communicable disease risk, teaches precautions, decides on exclusion and clearance of ill staff and supervises compliance.
Use standard precautions, report illness and exposures promptly and complete required training.

documentation: Risk category assignment for each position and employee
Orientation and annual training attendance records
Baseline TB screening record (Form DHHS 3405) and hepatitis B vaccination or declination records
Staff illness, exclusion and return-to-work records
Exposure incident reports
Dated annual policy review

policies.title: Bloodborne Pathogen Policy and Training
policies.applies_to: All hands-on in-home caregivers (in-home aides), service supervisors and registered nurses who may have contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials, and the Director.
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers, clients and the public from bloodborne disease by requiring training, safe work practices and protective equipment, and by keeping training records in each personnel file.
policies.policy: This policy meets the DHSR policy checklist item "Administrative Policies: bloodborne pathogen: Blood borne pathogen policy (include training and updates), required for all in-home caregivers." [AGENCY NAME] follows the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, which 10A NCAC 13J .1003(a) and (f)(6) incorporate through 29 CFR 1910. Every hands-on in-home caregiver must complete bloodborne pathogen training and airborne pathogen training before the first client assignment and every year after that. Training must follow the agency Exposure Control Plan (ADM-14). Training is repeated or updated whenever procedures, tasks or equipment change in a way that affects exposure risk. Each caregiver's training record is kept in the personnel file. The agency provides gloves and other protective equipment at no cost to the employee.

definitions.definition: Disease-causing microorganisms in human blood, including hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and HIV.
Body fluids such as semen, vaginal secretions, saliva in dental procedures, any body fluid visibly contaminated with blood, and all body fluids where blood and other fluids cannot be told apart.
Reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM while performing assigned duties.
Treating all blood and body fluids as if they were infectious.
Annual instruction on organisms spread through the air, such as tuberculosis, covering recognition, protective measures and reporting.

procedures: The Director and the Registered Nurse review every job category at least annually and list the tasks that could cause exposure to blood or OPIM (for example personal care with open skin, wound-area care, toileting, handling soiled linen, cleaning up spills, and handling a client's lancets or other sharps if found in the home). The list is recorded in the Exposure Control Plan (ADM-14).

Before a new hands-on caregiver is assigned to any client, [TRAINER NAME/TITLE], a person knowledgeable about the subject, provides bloodborne and airborne pathogen training as part of orientation (PER-06) and records the date in the personnel file.

Training covers: the OSHA standard and where to get a copy; the epidemiology and symptoms of bloodborne disease; how the viruses are spread; the agency Exposure Control Plan and how to get a copy; how to recognize tasks that may cause exposure; the use and limits of work practices and protective equipment; hepatitis B vaccine (ADM-13); what to do and whom to contact in an emergency or exposure incident; post-exposure evaluation and follow-up (ADM-14); and an opportunity for questions with the trainer.

Airborne pathogen training covers tuberculosis (ADM-12) and other respiratory infections, the signs and symptoms to report, respiratory etiquette, and when to notify the supervisor of illness or exposure.

Caregivers are taught to use universal precautions with every client: wash hands before and after care and after removing gloves; wear disposable gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items; cover cuts with a waterproof dressing; and use eye or face protection and a gown or apron when splashes are likely.

The agency supplies gloves, masks, eye protection, aprons, disinfectant, biohazard bags and a puncture-resistant sharps container to each caregiver at no cost. The service supervisor checks supplies during supervisory visits (CLN-08) and replaces them within [NUMBER] business days of a request.

Caregivers do not recap, bend or break needles, and do not pick up sharps by hand. Any sharp found in the home is moved only with tongs or a dustpan into a puncture-resistant container, and the supervisor is told. Caregivers do not give injections or perform tasks outside their permitted duties (CLN-13).

Caregivers clean blood or body fluid spills promptly with disposable towels and an EPA-registered disinfectant or a fresh 1:10 bleach solution. They bag soiled items, wash hands, and report the spill to the supervisor if there was any skin or mucous membrane contact.

Training is repeated at least once every 12 months. The Director schedules annual retraining and tracks due dates on the in-service tracking log (PER-05). A caregiver who is overdue is not scheduled for new hands-on assignments until the training is completed.

The Director or Registered Nurse updates the training content and retrains affected staff within [NUMBER] days whenever a new task, new equipment, a change in procedure or an exposure incident review shows a change is needed.

Each training record contains: the date; an outline of the content; the trainer's name and qualifications; the names and job titles of attendees; and the employee's signature. The record is filed in the personnel file (PRR-01).
Training records are kept in the personnel file for at least one year after termination, as required for personnel records, and for no less than three years from the training date.
The Director audits a sample of caregiver files each quarter to confirm that bloodborne and airborne training is current, and reports the results through the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and ensures resources for training and protective equipment.
Ensures all hands-on staff are trained before assignment and annually, keeps records, and maintains the supply budget.
Delivers or approves training content, observes safe practices during supervisory visits, and handles exposure reports.
Complete training, follow universal precautions, use protective equipment and report exposures and unsafe conditions immediately.

documentation: Bloodborne and airborne pathogen training record with date, content, trainer and signature, kept in each personnel file
Annual training due-date tracking log
Exposure determination (job category and task list) included in the Exposure Control Plan
Supply check notes from supervisory visits
Quarterly file audit results

policies.title: Tuberculosis (TB) Screening
policies.applies_to: All hands-on staff who provide in-home care, including in-home aides, nurses and supervisors who give hands-on care, before assignment to any client.
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of tuberculosis to clients, who are often elderly or medically fragile, by screening hands-on staff and keeping complete records.
policies.policy: This policy meets DHSR checklist item "Administrative Policies: .1003(b): TB (tuberculin skin test) policy, required for all in-home caregivers" and 10A NCAC 13J .1003(b). Every hands-on employee must have a baseline TB skin test, documented on Form DHHS 3405, before being assigned to any client. An employee whose test is positive must have documented noninfectious status before assignment. TB records are kept in the personnel file. No one provides hands-on care until this requirement is met.

definitions.definition: Any employee who has direct physical contact with clients in the home or who provides personal care.
The first tuberculin skin test recorded for an employee on Form DHHS 3405 before client assignment.
A written determination from a physician or other qualified health care provider that a person with a positive TB test does not have infectious TB disease.
The state tuberculosis screening form used to record the employee's TB test or screening result.

procedures: As part of the conditional job offer, [HUMAN RESOURCES/DIRECTOR] tells each hands-on applicant that a baseline TB skin test is required and that no client assignment can begin until the result is on file.

The Director arranges the TB skin test through [HEALTH CARE PROVIDER/CLINIC] before the first client assignment. Testing is arranged at the agency's expense unless the employee provides valid documentation of a recent result that the agency accepts under the rule.
The reading and result are recorded on Form DHHS 3405 and signed by the licensed person who administered and read the test. The employee also signs the form.
The Director or designee reviews Form DHHS 3405 for completeness (dates of placement and reading, result, signatures) before the employee is put on the schedule and records the review date.
If the skin test is negative, the employee may be assigned to clients once all other pre-assignment requirements are complete (PER-01 and PER-07).

If the skin test is positive, the employee is not assigned to clients until a physician or other qualified health care provider has evaluated the employee (including symptom review and any required chest X-ray) and has documented in writing that the employee is noninfectious. That documentation is filed with Form DHHS 3405.
An employee with a prior documented positive test does not repeat the skin test. The employee provides the prior result and the written noninfectious determination, and the Director files both.

The employee must report to the supervisor immediately any cough lasting more than three weeks, bloody sputum, unexplained weight loss, fever or night sweats. The supervisor removes the employee from client contact until a health care provider clears the employee in writing.

As agency practice, the service supervisor reviews TB symptoms at the annual performance evaluation (PER-04). After a known exposure to a person with infectious TB, the employee is referred for evaluation and retesting according to the advice of the local health department or the employee's provider.

If a client or household member is known to have infectious TB, the supervisor consults the local health department and follows its direction on staff protection before sending any caregiver to the home.

TB records are medical information. They are filed in the personnel file in the confidential health section, shared only with those who need them for compliance, and kept for at least one year after the employee leaves (ADM-15).
During the Personnel Record Review (PRR-01) the Director confirms each hands-on file contains Form DHHS 3405, and the noninfectious documentation where the test was positive.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures no hands-on staff member is assigned to a client before TB screening requirements are met and files are complete.
Reviews TB documentation, screens for symptoms, and removes symptomatic staff from client contact.
Completes testing, provides records, and reports symptoms or exposures promptly.

documentation: Form DHHS 3405 for each hands-on employee
Written noninfectious determination for any employee with a positive result
Documentation of any post-exposure evaluation or clearance after symptoms
Date the Director reviewed the TB record before first assignment

policies.title: Hepatitis B Immunization or Declination
policies.applies_to: All employees whose jobs involve reasonably anticipated exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, including all hands-on in-home caregivers.
policies.purpose: To offer every at-risk employee protection against hepatitis B at no cost and to document each employee's choice.
policies.policy: This policy meets DHSR checklist item "Administrative Policies: Hepatitis B: Hepatitis B immunization / declination policy, required for all in-home caregivers." [AGENCY NAME] offers the hepatitis B vaccine series to all at-risk employees at no cost to them, as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 and the infection control requirements of 10A NCAC 13J .1003. Each personnel file must contain either a vaccination record or a signed declination. An employee who declines may change their mind and receive the vaccine later at no cost.

definitions.definition: An employee in a job category listed in the Exposure Control Plan as having occupational exposure to blood or OPIM.
A signed statement by an employee who has been offered the vaccine and chooses not to take it, using the OSHA-required wording.
Documentation of vaccine doses received, with dates and the name of the provider, or proof of immunity from a prior series or antibody testing.

procedures: During orientation (PER-06) and after bloodborne pathogen training (ADM-11), the Director or Registered Nurse explains hepatitis B, the vaccine's safety and effectiveness, how it is given, and that it is free to the employee.

The agency offers the vaccine series to each at-risk employee within 10 working days of initial assignment to a job with exposure risk, unless the employee already has documented immunity, the vaccine is medically contraindicated, or the employee has previously completed the series.

Vaccination is provided under the supervision of a licensed health care professional at [HEALTH CARE PROVIDER/CLINIC], at a reasonable time and place, with no cost and no loss of pay for the employee.

If the employee accepts, the Director gives the employee a referral, tracks the dates of each dose, and files the provider's vaccination record in the personnel file. Booster doses are offered only if recommended by the U.S. Public Health Service.
If the employee has already been vaccinated, the employee provides the written record or lab proof of immunity. The Director files it and notes that the offer was made and not needed.

If the employee declines, the employee signs and dates the hepatitis B declination form stating that the vaccine was offered, that remaining unvaccinated carries a risk of hepatitis B, and that the vaccine can still be accepted later at no cost. The declination is filed in the personnel file.

An employee who declined may request the vaccine at any time while still in an at-risk job. The Director arranges it within 10 working days of the request and replaces the declination with the vaccination record in the file.
If an employee has an exposure incident (ADM-14) and is unvaccinated, the post-exposure evaluation includes a new offer of the vaccine as directed by the health care provider.

Vaccination and declination records are confidential medical records (ADM-15). They are kept in the personnel file's confidential health section for at least one year after termination, and the medical record is retained for the length required by the OSHA standard for employee medical records.
The Director checks that every hands-on caregiver's file contains a vaccination record or signed declination during the annual file audit and the Personnel Record Review (PRR-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the vaccine is offered within the required time, pays for vaccination, and files records.
Educates employees about hepatitis B and the vaccine and answers questions.
Accepts the vaccine or signs a declination, and may request the vaccine later.

documentation: Hepatitis B vaccination record or proof of immunity
Signed hepatitis B declination form
Date of offer and any later request for the vaccine
Annual file audit results

policies.title: Exposure Control Plan and Post-Exposure Follow-Up
policies.applies_to: All employees with occupational exposure risk, including in-home aides, nurses and supervisors; the Director and Registered Nurse who maintain the plan.
policies.purpose: To set out how the agency identifies exposure risks, controls them, and responds to any exposure to blood, body fluids or airborne pathogens, so that employees get prompt care and confidential follow-up.
policies.policy: This policy meets DHSR checklist item "Administrative Policies: .1003(a) exposure control: Exposure control plan & Post exposure follow-up plan policy." As required by 10A NCAC 13J .1003(a), which incorporates 29 CFR 1910, and 29 CFR 1910.1030, [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Exposure Control Plan that lists the job categories at risk and the controls used. After any exposure incident, the employee receives immediate first aid, reports to the supervisor, and is offered medical evaluation and confidential follow-up. Each exposure incident is documented, and the plan is reviewed at least annually.

definitions.definition: A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM, such as a needle stick, that results from the performance of an employee's duties. Contact with a person with suspected infectious TB is also handled under this policy.
The client or other person whose blood or body fluids were the source of the exposure.
Items and practices that reduce exposure, such as sharps containers, hand hygiene, no recapping, and cleaning methods.
The agency's written plan identifying who is at risk and how risk is reduced and managed.

procedures: The Director and Registered Nurse write and maintain the Exposure Control Plan. It contains: the exposure determination listing every job category and the tasks with occupational exposure; the schedule and methods for implementing the OSHA standard; the controls used (universal precautions, personal protective equipment, hand hygiene, sharps handling, spill clean-up, laundry and waste handling); the hepatitis B vaccine program (ADM-13); training (ADM-11); and post-exposure procedures.
A copy of the plan is available to every employee in the office and given to any employee who asks within 15 working days of the request.

The plan is reviewed and updated at least once a year and whenever tasks, procedures or equipment change. The review considers available safer devices and input from caregivers who do the work. The Director dates and signs each review.

Immediately after an exposure, the employee takes first aid: wash needle sticks, cuts and skin with soap and water; flush splashes to the nose, mouth or skin with water; irrigate eyes with clean water or saline.

The employee reports the exposure to [SERVICE SUPERVISOR NAME/PHONE] immediately, during the same shift and before leaving the client, if it is safe. If the supervisor cannot be reached, the employee calls [AFTER-HOURS PHONE]. Reporting is never grounds for discipline.

The supervisor, on the day of the report, directs the employee to the medical provider [HEALTH CARE PROVIDER/CLINIC/EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT] for immediate evaluation. The agency pays for the evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee.

The supervisor completes an Exposure Incident Report documenting the date and time, the task being done, the route of exposure, the personal protective equipment used, the source individual (named only on the confidential report), and the first aid given.

The agency tries to identify the source individual and, where the client or the client's representative consents, asks for testing for HBV, HCV and HIV, respecting state law and client rights (CLN-01). The result is given to the exposed employee's health care provider. If consent is not obtained, that is documented.

The exposed employee receives confidential medical evaluation and follow-up from the health care provider, including counseling, baseline and follow-up testing, post-exposure prophylaxis when indicated, and hepatitis B vaccine if the employee is not already immune.

Within 15 days after the evaluation is complete, the agency obtains the health care professional's written opinion. The opinion given to the agency is limited to whether the hepatitis B vaccine is indicated and whether the employee received it, and confirmation that the employee has been told the evaluation results. The employee receives a copy.
For an exposure to a person with suspected or confirmed infectious TB or other airborne disease, the supervisor consults the local health department and refers the employee for evaluation (ADM-12).
The Director reviews each exposure within 5 business days to identify the cause and corrective action, including retraining (ADM-11), and records the corrective action.

The agency records needlestick and sharps injuries on a sharps injury log as required by OSHA, protecting the employee's identity, and if the exposure involves a work injury, also files for workers' compensation.

Exposure records and medical records are kept confidential (ADM-15) and not disclosed without the employee's written consent except as required by law. They are retained as OSHA requires for employee medical records, and the incident report is also entered into incident tracking (CLN-15).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the plan, ensures annual review, pays for evaluation and follow-up, and maintains confidential records.
Receives exposure reports, arranges same-day medical evaluation, completes the report and requests source testing where consent is given.
Use controls, give first aid, and report all exposures immediately.

documentation: Written Exposure Control Plan with annual review signature and date
Exposure Incident Report
Health care professional's written opinion
Sharps injury log
Corrective action record following each exposure
Confidential medical records kept separate from the general personnel file

policies.title: Employee and Client Confidentiality (HIPAA)
policies.applies_to: All employees, caregivers, contractors, volunteers, governing body members and anyone with access to client or employee information.
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of clients and employees, control disclosure of records, and ensure clients are told of their right to object before information is released or records are inspected.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(10), employee and client confidentiality (item A(10)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps all client and employee information confidential and complies with the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, including 45 CFR 164.530 on administrative requirements). Under G.S. 131E-141, before releasing information or allowing record inspection, the agency advises each client in writing of the right to object in writing. The agency also gives each client written notice of the DHSR hotline number before care starts or at the initial evaluation visit. DHHS may inspect client records at the agency to investigate alleged violations and must keep complainants and inspected records confidential (G.S. 131E-144.7). A privacy official is designated and all staff are trained. Employee personnel and health information is also confidential.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a client, in any form, including name, address, diagnosis, care plan and visit notes.
The person designated by the governing body to develop and carry out privacy policies and receive privacy complaints.
Using or sharing only the least information needed for the purpose.
Acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI in a way not permitted by the Privacy Rule that compromises its security or privacy.

procedures: The governing body designates [PRIVACY OFFICIAL NAME/TITLE] as privacy official and records the designation in the governing body minutes. The privacy official's contact information is [PHONE] and [ADDRESS].

At the initial evaluation visit and before care begins, the Registered Nurse or service supervisor gives each client the Notice of Privacy Practices and a written notice of the right to object in writing to release of information or to record inspection. The client or representative signs an acknowledgment, which is filed in the client record (CLN-12, with signed rights form).
At the same time, the nurse or supervisor gives the client written notice of the DHSR hotline number, [DHSR HOTLINE NUMBER AS PUBLISHED BY DHSR], and documents the date given (CLN-02).

Before any release of client information outside treatment, payment and operations, the privacy official checks the client's written objection or signed authorization. If the client has objected in writing, the information is not released except as required by law.

Records may be released without client authorization only as permitted by HIPAA and state law, such as to DHSR surveyors, to Medicaid or its agents, in required abuse or neglect reports, or to emergency responders. The privacy official logs each disclosure that must be tracked and applies the minimum necessary standard.

When DHHS inspects client records at the agency to investigate an alleged violation, the Director provides access, tells the client in advance where required, and notes the inspection in the disclosure log. The agency will not disclose or try to learn the identity of any complainant, and DHHS is responsible for keeping complainants and inspected records confidential.

All staff receive confidentiality and HIPAA training during orientation (PER-06) before accessing records and receive refresher training each year (PER-05). Staff sign a confidentiality agreement, filed in the personnel file.

Staff access only the information needed for their job. Paper records are in locked cabinets in the office, and electronic records are protected by individual passwords, access controls, encryption and automatic log-off. Shared passwords are prohibited.

Caregivers do not discuss clients in public, with other clients or on social media. They never post client names, photos, addresses, descriptions or any information that could identify a client on any social media platform, even without a name.

Caregivers do not send PHI by personal text message, personal email or messaging apps. Communication about clients uses only the agency-approved secure methods: [APPROVED SECURE APP/PHONE LINE]. A text limited to schedule logistics with no clinical detail or full name, such as running late, is permitted.

Records kept in the client's home, such as the plan of care and the visit log, remain in the home in a place agreed with the client, are not removed except as approved by the supervisor, and are never left in vehicles or shared with visitors. Caregivers return completed documentation to the office on the schedule set by the supervisor.

Employee information is confidential. Personnel files, background checks, performance evaluations and payroll data are kept in locked or access-restricted files. Employee health records, including TB, hepatitis B and exposure records, are kept in a separate confidential health section, and shared only as needed for compliance or required by law (ADM-12, ADM-13, ADM-14).

Any employee who suspects an impermissible use or disclosure reports it to the privacy official immediately. The privacy official investigates, documents, mitigates harm, and, if the incident is a reportable breach, notifies affected clients without unreasonable delay and within 60 days of discovery and meets other notice requirements in 45 CFR Part 164.
Violations lead to discipline up to termination under the progressive discipline policy. No one is retaliated against for reporting a privacy concern (PER-09).
The privacy official reviews this policy annually, along with security risk analysis results, and reports to the governing body (ADM-16). Records are retained as required by CLN-12 and PER-03.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, designates the privacy official and reviews privacy reports.
Maintains policies, trains staff, manages authorizations, objections and disclosure logs, investigates breaches and receives privacy complaints.
Ensures safeguards are in place and cooperates with DHSR record inspections.
Protect client and employee information, follow secure communication rules and report suspected violations immediately.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of Notice of Privacy Practices
Signed notice of right to object in writing to release of information and record inspection
Documentation of DHSR hotline number notice given to the client
Confidentiality agreement signed by each employee
HIPAA training records
Disclosure log and written client objections or authorizations
Breach investigation and notification records
Governing body minutes designating the privacy official

policies.title: Policy Review and Document Control
policies.applies_to: The governing body, Director, Registered Nurse, service supervisors and all staff who use the Policy & Procedure Manual.
policies.purpose: To make sure the policies required by 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a) are adopted by the governing body, reviewed at least annually, controlled by version, and available to staff and surveyors.
policies.policy: The governing body of [AGENCY NAME] adopts the written policies required by 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a): scope of services, admission and discharge, supervision, plan of care, emergency care in the home, record return timeframe, personnel qualifications, organizational chart, program evaluation, confidentiality and referrals. The governing body reviews all policies at least annually, and the review is informed by the annual program evaluation required by 10A NCAC 13J .1004. A version log records every adoption and revision with its date and approval. The manual is kept available to all staff and is made available immediately to DHSR surveyors on request.

definitions.definition: The owner or board with legal authority and responsibility for the agency and for adopting its policies.
A table listing each policy's number, title, version, effective date, summary of change and approval date.
The current approved version of the manual, available in print and/or electronic form, and identified by version and date.

procedures: The Director maintains the master Policy & Procedure Manual with a table of contents, policy numbers, a version log and a header on each page showing policy ID, version number and effective date.

The governing body adopts the initial manual by vote recorded in its minutes, showing the date, the policies adopted and the signature of the governing body chair. Policies for all 11 topics in 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a) must be adopted before the agency begins services.

At least once every 12 months, on [REVIEW MONTH], the governing body reviews every policy in the manual. The Director prepares a review packet showing each policy, any rule or program changes, and the results of the annual program evaluation (ADM-08) and the 90-day record reviews (ADM-09) that suggest changes.

Before each annual review, the Director checks the current 10A NCAC 13J rule text and DHSR notices for changes, and the Medicaid clinical coverage policies, the HIPAA rules and OSHA standards, and notes any needed revisions.
The governing body records in its minutes that each policy was reviewed and whether it was approved without change, revised or retired, and the chair signs and dates the minutes.

When a policy is revised outside the annual cycle, for example after a rule change, a survey finding or a plan of correction (SUP-02), the Director drafts the revision, the governing body approves it in writing, and the version log is updated with the date and approval.

The Director assigns a new version number and effective date to each revised policy, removes superseded copies from circulation and keeps the prior version in an archive file with a "superseded" mark for at least [NUMBER] years.

Within [NUMBER] business days of approval, the Director informs affected staff of each change in writing, trains them if procedures change, and obtains staff signatures acknowledging the change. The acknowledgment is filed in each personnel file.

A complete current copy of the manual is kept at the agency office at [ADDRESS] where all staff can read it during working hours. Electronic access is given to staff through [SECURE SYSTEM] and a printed copy is available to caregivers who ask.

The manual must be produced immediately for DHSR surveyors, without delay, during any survey, inspection or complaint investigation. The Director or the person in charge at the office knows where it is kept. A copy of the version log and governing body minutes showing the latest review is kept with it.
New staff are shown where the manual is kept and how to find the policies relevant to their job during orientation (PER-06).

Policies that carry a signed form requirement, such as client rights and consent to release information, are updated at the same time as their forms, and the Director confirms forms in use match the current version.

The Director audits the manual every quarter to confirm that only current versions are in use, the log is accurate, and the 11 required policy topics are all present, and reports exceptions to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts, reviews at least annually, and approves all policies and revisions, and records its action in the minutes.
Maintains the manual and version log, prepares review packets, distributes revisions and ensures surveyor access.
Recommend policy changes from clinical experience and train staff on revisions.
Know where the manual is, follow current policies and sign acknowledgments of changes.

documentation: Governing body minutes showing initial adoption and annual review of each policy
Version log with dates and approvals
Archive of superseded policies
Staff acknowledgment of policy changes
Quarterly manual audit notes

policies.title: Compliance, Fraud Prevention, Billing Integrity and Administrative Records
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Agency Director, Service Supervisor, office/billing staff, scheduling staff, and all in-home aides and nurses
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] obeys all federal, state and local law, prevents false claims and illegal kickbacks, bills only for services actually delivered, keeps the administrative, financial and statistical records North Carolina requires, and keeps its staff credentials current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with all federal, state and local laws that apply to a licensed home care agency. This includes the false-statement and kickback provisions of Section 1128B of the Social Security Act and 42 USC 1320a-7a and 1320a-7b, as required by 10A NCAC 13J .0906. The agency does not make false statements or submit false claims to Medicaid or any other payer. It does not offer, pay, solicit or accept anything of value in exchange for client referrals or for arranging services. Every staff member must hold a current North Carolina license or registration for the work he or she performs. The agency keeps the annual home care budget and statistical records (staff full-time equivalents, client demographics, units of service) available for inspection and retains them for at least 3 years, as required by 10A NCAC 13J .1002. If [AGENCY NAME] is part of a larger entity, home care finances are kept separately identifiable. If the agency is accredited and deemed licensed under G.S. 131E-138(g), it sends DHSR copies of accreditation survey reports within 30 days. This policy supports the agency's licensure obligations under 10A NCAC 13J .0906 and .1002 and G.S. 131E-138(g).

definitions.definition: Any bill, record, time entry or statement to a payer or regulator that the agency knows, or should know, is untrue. Examples are billing for a visit that did not occur, billing more hours than worked, or billing for a service not authorized or not in the plan of care.
Anything of value offered, paid, solicited or received to induce or reward referrals of clients or the ordering or arranging of services paid for by a federal health care program.
Records of staff full-time equivalents, client demographics and units of service.
Treatment of an accredited agency as licensed, without further review, for all services it provides, under G.S. 131E-138(g) and Commission rules.
The person designated by the governing body to oversee this policy. Unless the governing body names someone else, this is the Agency Director, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

procedures: The governing body designates the Agency Director as Compliance Officer in writing. The designation is recorded in governing body minutes and reviewed each year at the program evaluation (ADM-08).

At hire and at least annually, the Compliance Officer trains every employee on this policy. The training covers false claims, kickbacks, accurate documentation and how to report concerns. Staff sign an attendance and acknowledgment form that is filed in the personnel record.

Every employee signs a code-of-conduct acknowledgment stating that he or she will not falsify visit notes, time records or EVV entries and will not accept payment or gifts for referrals (see CLN-16 and PER-09).

Before billing any visit, billing staff confirm that the visit was authorized (or covered by a signed service agreement for private pay), is in the plan of care, was delivered by a qualified aide, and is supported by a dated and signed service entry and, for Medicaid, an EVV record (MED-03).
Billing staff never bill for missed, cancelled or unverified visits. The Service Supervisor resolves visit discrepancies in writing before the claim or invoice is released.

The Compliance Officer reviews a sample of claims and invoices each quarter against visit notes, timesheets and authorizations. The review is documented with the sample size, findings and corrections. Findings go to the governing body at least annually.

If the agency finds it was overpaid or billed in error, the Compliance Officer stops further billing for the issue, corrects it, and reports and returns the overpayment to the payer as that payer's rules require. The steps are documented.

The agency does not pay or give anything of value for referrals and does not accept payment for referring clients. Marketing and community-agency relationships (CLN-03) are reviewed by the Compliance Officer to confirm they involve no remuneration for referrals.

As agency practice, the Compliance Officer screens all employees and contractors against federal and state exclusion lists at hire and monthly. A person who appears on a list is removed from any duty that is billed to a federal health care program, and the Compliance Officer reviews the finding with the governing body.

At hire and at each renewal date, the Agency Director verifies that every licensed or registered staff member holds a current North Carolina license or registration (PER-01). The verification is dated and filed. Staff whose credential lapses are removed from duties requiring it until renewal is verified.

Any employee who suspects a false claim, kickback or other violation reports it to the Compliance Officer, or to the governing body if the concern involves the Compliance Officer. No one is retaliated against for a good-faith report.

The Compliance Officer opens a written inquiry within 2 business days of a report, documents the investigation and decides on corrective action. Corrective action can include retraining, discipline, repayment or referral to the proper authority.
Each year the Agency Director prepares the home care budget and files it in the administrative records. The agency keeps it available for DHSR inspection.

The Agency Director maintains statistical records covering staff full-time equivalents, client demographics and units of service, updated at least monthly and summarized each year for the program evaluation (ADM-08).

If [AGENCY NAME] is part of a larger organization, the Agency Director confirms that the home care budget, revenue and expenses are tracked in separate accounts or cost centers so that home care finances can be identified separately on inspection.

The agency retains the budget and statistical records for at least 3 years. Where another law, payer contract or Medicaid requirement calls for a longer period, the longer period applies. Records are stored securely and are not destroyed without the Compliance Officer's written approval.

If the agency is accredited, the Agency Director sends DHSR a copy of each accreditation survey report within 30 days of receiving it and files the transmittal. The agency tells DHSR about any accreditation change as described in SUP-02.
The Agency Director reviews this policy at the annual policy review (ADM-16) and updates it for any change in law or payer rules.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, designates the Compliance Officer, reviews compliance findings at least annually and supports corrective action.
Trains staff, audits billing, verifies credentials, screens for exclusions, investigates reports, keeps the budget and statistical records, and sends accreditation reports to DHSR within 30 days.
Bill only verified, authorized services, and escalate discrepancies before billing.
Reconciles visit documentation and EVV exceptions and reports suspected falsification.
Document honestly, refuse kickbacks, keep credentials current and report suspected violations.

documentation: Governing body designation of Compliance Officer
Staff compliance training attendance and acknowledgment forms
Code-of-conduct acknowledgments
Quarterly billing audit worksheets and corrective actions
Overpayment and refund records
Exclusion screening logs
Credential and license verification records
Compliance inquiry files
Annual home care budget
Statistical records (FTEs, client demographics, units of service), retained at least 3 years
Separate home care financial records
Accreditation survey report transmittals to DHSR (if applicable)

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Agency Director, Service Supervisor, RN/assessing practitioner, and all in-home aides and office staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every client of [AGENCY NAME] is told about, understands and can exercise the rights guaranteed by North Carolina law, and knows his or her responsibilities, from the first contact.
policies.policy: This policy meets Client Care Policies item .1007(a)(b); 131E-144.3: Client's rights and responsibilities policy (including G.S. 131E-144.3). Under 10A NCAC 13J .1007, [AGENCY NAME] gives each client written notice of the client's rights and responsibilities before care begins or at the initial evaluation visit. The notice includes the full Declaration of Home Care Clients' Rights in G.S. 131E-144.3, which has 15 rights. They include the right to participate in the plan of care; to be treated with dignity and privacy; to confidentiality; to be free from abuse, neglect and exploitation; to voice grievances without reprisal; to a written statement of charges; to refuse services; to reach the on-call staff member and a supervisor; and to notice of license action against the agency within the timeframe set in the statute. At the same time, as required by G.S. 131E-144.4, the agency gives the client its client-responsibility policies, the agency complaint contact, and the address and telephone number of the DHSR Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section (919-855-4620). The agency documents that the client was informed and keeps a signed receipt in the client record. Under G.S. 131E-144.5 the Agency Director is responsible for implementing the Bill of Rights, and the agency trains all staff to implement it. For Medicaid clients, these rights are applied consistently with home and community-based settings protections (42 CFR 441.301(c)) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

definitions.term: Declaration of Home Care Clients' Rights
definitions.definition: The 15 rights listed in G.S. 131E-144.3.
The first in-home visit by the agency's RN or practitioner to assess the client (CLN-05).
A form signed and dated by the client or representative acknowledging that the rights, responsibilities and contact notices were received and explained.
A legal guardian, health care or general power-of-attorney agent, or other person legally authorized to act for the client.

procedures: Before the first aide visit, and no later than the initial evaluation visit, the RN or Service Supervisor gives the client (and representative, if any) the Client Rights and Responsibilities packet. The packet holds the full text of G.S. 131E-144.3, the client responsibilities, the agency complaint contact ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]), the DHSR section address ([ADDRESS OF DHSR SECTION, verified before printing]) and phone number (919-855-4620), and the DHSR hotline notice (CLN-02).

The staff member reads or reviews the rights with the client in plain language. For clients with limited English proficiency, a hearing or vision impairment, or a cognitive impairment, the staff member uses the accommodations in CLN-17 (interpreter, large print, alternate format) so the client understands.

The staff member explains each of the 15 rights and gives examples of how the agency honors them, including that the client may take part in planning care, refuse any service, ask for a different aide, and reach an on-call staff member and a supervisor at any time.

The staff member explains the client's responsibilities. These include giving accurate health and contact information, telling the agency about changes in condition or hospitalization, providing a reasonably safe home, treating staff with respect, not offering gifts or money to staff (CLN-16), observing the no-smoking policy (CLN-07), and giving notice of cancelled visits.
The client or representative signs and dates the receipt. The staff member also signs and dates it, and records the way the rights were explained (in person, interpreter, etc.).
If the client cannot or will not sign, the staff member documents the reason, the date and a witness, and tries again at the next visit. Services are not delayed in a way that harms the client.
The staff member leaves a complete copy of the packet with the client and files the signed receipt in the client record within 2 business days (CLN-12).
The Service Supervisor checks at the start of service that a signed receipt is on file for every client. Any missing receipt is obtained at the next supervisory visit (CLN-08).
The Agency Director gives each client written notice when the agency's rights or contact information changes, and gives every client an updated packet when a rights document is revised.
The agency posts or provides the client rights notice where it will be seen by clients and visitors, including the office.

The Agency Director trains all new employees on the Bill of Rights during orientation (PER-06), before they provide care. Aides and nurses are retrained during in-service education each year (PER-05). Attendance and a short competency check are documented.

Staff who see or learn of a possible rights violation report it to the Service Supervisor or Agency Director the same day. The Director investigates under CLN-02, and any abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled under CLN-14.
The Agency Director reviews rights complaints and training records at each annual program evaluation (ADM-08) and corrects any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Is responsible for implementing the Bill of Rights, ensures staff training, and investigates rights violations.
Delivers and explains the rights packet at the initial evaluation visit and obtains the signed receipt.
Confirms a signed receipt is on file, reinforces rights at supervisory visits and addresses staff conduct concerns.
Honor client rights at every visit and report concerns right away.
Reads or has explained the notice and follows the stated client responsibilities.

documentation: Signed and dated Client Rights and Responsibilities receipt in the client record
Copy of the packet version given (date and version number)
Notes on interpreter or accommodation used
Staff training attendance and competency records on the Bill of Rights
Rights-related complaint and investigation files

policies.title: Client Complaints and Grievances (with DHSR Hotline)
policies.applies_to: Agency Director, Service Supervisor, RN, office staff and all in-home aides
policies.purpose: To give clients and families a simple way to raise complaints, to make sure each complaint is investigated within 72 hours and documented, and to protect clients from reprisal.
policies.policy: This policy meets Client Care Policies item .1007(b)(c); 131E-144.6(b): Agency complaint policy with state hotline number(s). [AGENCY NAME] welcomes complaints from clients, families and representatives. The agency investigates each client or family complaint within 72 hours of receiving it and documents the complaint and its resolution, as required by G.S. 131E-144.6(b). Under 10A NCAC 13J .1007 and G.S. 131E-141(c), each client receives written notice of the DHSR hotline number before care begins or at the initial evaluation visit. Clients may call the DHSR hotline at any time, whether or not they have complained to the agency first. The hotline number to be printed on the client notice is 1-800-624-3004. The Agency Director confirms the current number with DHSR before each printing. The DHSR Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section may also be reached at 919-855-4620. Under G.S. 131E-144.3, clients may voice grievances without reprisal. No client is threatened, penalized, or given reduced or changed service because he or she complained. The Agency Director is the complaint contact: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE].

definitions.definition: Any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction or concern from a client, family member or representative about services, staff, billing or the agency.
A complaint that is not resolved at first contact or that involves rights, safety, or the conduct of staff.
Any retaliation against a client or staff member for complaining, including reduced service, a change of aide, threats or discharge.
The toll-free line (1-800-624-3004, to be confirmed before printing) through which anyone can file a complaint with the NC Division of Health Service Regulation.

procedures: Before care begins or at the initial evaluation visit, the RN or Service Supervisor gives the client a written notice of the DHSR hotline number (1-800-624-3004, confirmed against the current DHSR number before printing), the DHSR section phone (919-855-4620), and the agency complaint contact ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]). The staff member explains that the client may complain to the agency, to DHSR or to both, at any time, without reprisal.
The client signs the receipt for the notice (CLN-01), and the signed receipt is filed in the client record.

Any employee who receives a complaint (by phone, in person, in writing or through an aide) records it the same day on the Complaint/Grievance Form. The form shows the date and time, who made it, the client, the allegation, and who took it. Staff do not discourage a complaint or ask the client to withdraw it.

The employee gives the complaint to the Agency Director or Service Supervisor within 1 business day, or immediately if the complaint involves abuse, neglect, exploitation, an injury, or a safety risk.
The Agency Director or designee acknowledges the complaint to the complainant, by phone or in writing, and logs it in the Complaint Log with a tracking number.

If a client may be in danger, the Agency Director takes immediate protective action (for example, removing the involved staff member from the client's schedule, arranging a nurse visit, or calling 911). Abuse, neglect and exploitation allegations are also handled under CLN-14, and any substantiated or suspected misconduct involving a nurse aide or other covered staff is handled under CLN-11.

The Agency Director begins the investigation immediately and completes it within 72 hours of receiving the complaint. The investigation includes interviewing the complainant, the client, the staff involved and any witnesses, and reviewing the client record, visit notes, schedule and EVV data.

The Agency Director documents the findings, the conclusion and the action taken to resolve the complaint on the complaint form. Actions can include retraining, discipline, changing a schedule, adjusting the plan of care with the RN, or an apology and refund.

The Agency Director tells the complainant of the result and any action taken, orally and in writing, within the same 72-hour window where possible. If more time is truly required to resolve the problem itself, the Director tells the complainant, documents the reason, and documents interim steps taken. The 72-hour investigation requirement is not extended.

The agency tells the client again, in writing, that he or she may contact the DHSR hotline or the DHSR section (919-855-4620) if not satisfied. The agency does not require a client to use the agency process first.

No staff member may retaliate against a client who complains. A report of suspected reprisal is investigated by the Agency Director (or the governing body if the Director is involved), and violators are disciplined up to and including termination.

When DHSR investigates a complaint, the Agency Director cooperates fully and gives surveyors access to records. Before releasing client information or permitting a record inspection, the agency advises each client in writing of the client's right to object in writing (G.S. 131E-141(b)). The client's written objection or acknowledgment is filed in the record.

DHSR may begin its own investigation immediately for life-threatening situations, within 24 hours for abuse, within 48 hours for neglect, and within 2 weeks for other complaints (G.S. 131E-144.6). The Agency Director makes sure that someone with authority is available to cooperate with surveyors during those times.
If DHSR cites a deficiency from a complaint, the agency prepares and submits its plan of correction as described in SUP-02.
The Agency Director reviews the Complaint Log at least quarterly, looking for trends, and presents a summary at the annual program evaluation (ADM-08). Corrective actions are tracked to completion.

responsibilities.duty: Is the complaint contact, completes and documents each investigation within 72 hours, protects against reprisal and cooperates with DHSR.
Receives complaints from aides and clients, escalates the same day, and helps investigate.
Reviews care-related complaints and adjusts the plan of care as needed.
Accept and report complaints without discouraging them or retaliating.
Keep the hotline notice current, log complaints and keep the Complaint Log.

documentation: Signed receipt for hotline and complaint-contact notice in the client record
Complaint/Grievance Form with date, investigation notes, findings and resolution
Complaint Log with tracking numbers and dates received and resolved
Written response to complainant
Written notice to clients of the right to object to release of information or record inspection
Quarterly trend review and annual evaluation summary
DHSR correspondence and plans of correction

policies.title: Coordination of and Referral To and From Community Agencies
policies.applies_to: Agency Director, Service Supervisor, RN, intake staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] coordinates care with other community agencies and resources, accepts referrals appropriately, and refers clients elsewhere when the agency cannot meet their needs.
policies.policy: This policy meets Client Care Policies item .1001(a)(11) & .1101(8): Coordination and referral policy, and item A(11), coordination of and referral to and from other community agencies and resources (10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(11)). [AGENCY NAME] works with other community agencies and resources to meet client needs and avoid duplicating services. When the agency cannot meet a client's needs, it notifies the referral source and refers the client to other agencies, as required by 10A NCAC 13J .1101. Each referral and coordination contact is documented in the client record. The agency keeps a current community resource list that includes the county Department of Social Services (DSS), the Area Agency on Aging, NCLIFTSS (CAP/DA referral and assessment entity, 833-522-5429), hospitals and hospice providers. Information about a client is shared with another agency only with the client's authorization or as otherwise permitted by law (ADM-15).

definitions.definition: A request from a person or organization (for example a hospital, physician, DSS, NCLIFTSS or family member) that the agency evaluate a person for services.
The agency's action in directing a client or referral source to another agency or resource that can meet a need the agency cannot.
Sharing information and planning with other providers to make sure services fit together.
The person or organization that asked the agency to evaluate or serve a client.

procedures: The Agency Director maintains a Community Resource List that includes the county DSS (including Adult Protective Services), the local Area Agency on Aging, NCLIFTSS (833-522-5429), area hospitals and discharge planners, hospice providers, home health agencies, adult day programs, and other in-home aide agencies. Each entry shows the contact name, phone number and services offered. The list is reviewed and updated at least every 6 months.
Intake staff record every referral to the agency on the Referral Log, showing the date, referral source, contact information, and the reason for the referral.

At intake, staff ask about other agencies or providers already serving the client (for example home health, hospice, CAP/DA case management) and, with the client's written authorization (ADM-15), contact them to coordinate so that visits, tasks and plans of care do not conflict.
The RN decides, using CLN-04 and CLN-05, whether the agency can meet the client's needs with its staffing, scope of services (ADM-01) and service area (ADM-03).

If the agency cannot meet the client's needs, the Service Supervisor notifies the referral source promptly, and no later than 2 business days after the decision. The notice says why. It is made by phone or in writing, and the call or letter is documented.

When the agency cannot serve a person, staff also refer the person or family to at least one other appropriate agency or resource from the Community Resource List. Staff provide names and phone numbers and, if the client agrees, make the contact for the client.

When a client already served by the agency has needs beyond its scope (for example skilled nursing, therapy, hospice, adult day services, or a need for protective services), the RN or Service Supervisor discusses referral options with the client or representative and makes the referral with consent.
When a client's need involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, staff follow CLN-14 and report to DSS as required, rather than using the routine referral process.

When a client is hospitalized, transferred or discharged, the Service Supervisor coordinates with the hospital, facility or receiving agency, sending needed information (with authorization) so services continue safely (CLN-10).
For Medicaid clients, the Service Supervisor coordinates with NCLIFTSS, the CAP/DA case manager or the PCS assessor about authorization, plan of care changes and unmet needs (MED-01, MED-02).

Staff document every referral made or received and every coordination contact in the client record. The entry shows the date, the person contacted, the agency, the information shared, the outcome and the staff member's signature.
The Agency Director reviews the Referral Log annually as part of the program evaluation (ADM-08) to evaluate how well referrals worked and to identify unmet community needs.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the community resource list, builds agency relationships and reviews referral outcomes.
Notifies referral sources, makes referrals to other agencies and coordinates with other providers.
Determines whether needs can be met and makes clinical referrals.
Log referrals and keep resource contacts current.

documentation: Community Resource List with revision dates
Referral Log (received and made)
Client record entries for each coordination or referral contact
Notice to referral source when needs cannot be met
Signed authorizations to share information
Annual referral review in program evaluation

policies.title: Acceptance of Clients for Service
policies.applies_to: Agency Director, Service Supervisor, RN, intake and scheduling staff
policies.purpose: To set written intake criteria so [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose needs it can safely meet, and handles reductions, endings and referrals fairly.
policies.policy: This policy meets Client Care Policies item .1101(1-8): Acceptance of Clients for Service Provision (10A NCAC 13J .1101), and, together with CLN-10, item A(2): admission and discharge policies (10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(2)). [AGENCY NAME] accepts a person for service only after determining that: (a) it has adequate staff to provide the needed services, including coverage when a regular aide is absent; (b) the home is suitable for safe care; (c) family or other caregiver availability has been considered; and (d) the needs fall within the agency's scope of services (ADM-01) and its geographic service area (ADM-03). When the agency cannot meet a person's needs, it notifies the referral source and refers the person to other agencies (CLN-03). The agency gives the client 48 hours' notice before reducing or ending service, subject to the exceptions listed in 10A NCAC 13J .1101. The in-home aide service area is limited to the agency's county, contiguous counties, or within 90 minutes' driving time, whichever is greater (10A NCAC 13J .1107(h)). The agency does not expand its service area without a new site until it has given DHSR 30 days' written notice (10A NCAC 13J .1001(g)). Acceptance is without discrimination (CLN-17).

definitions.definition: The Agency Director's or RN's decision, documented in writing, that the agency will serve a client, made after intake screening and the initial in-home assessment.
Whether the home environment (safety, sanitation, utilities, access, hazards, pets, smoking) allows aides to give care safely.
A plan to supply a qualified replacement aide when the assigned aide is sick, on leave or unavailable.
The geographic area named in policy ADM-03 within which the agency provides in-home aide services.

procedures: Intake staff take each inquiry or referral on the Intake Form. It records the client's name, address and phone, the referral source, the services requested, the payer (private pay, Medicaid State Plan PCS or CAP/DA), the hours sought and the client's preferred schedule.

Intake staff check the address against the service area in ADM-03 (agency county, contiguous counties or within 90 minutes' driving time, whichever is greater). Requests outside the area are declined and referred under CLN-03 before any assessment is scheduled.
