The Service Supervisor checks the requested services against the agency's scope (ADM-01) and permitted aide duties (CLN-13). Services outside the scope, such as skilled nursing tasks, are not accepted, and the client is referred under CLN-03.

The Service Supervisor confirms with scheduling staff that the agency has enough qualified staff to cover the requested hours and has a backup plan for absences (CLN-19). The result is written on the Intake Form. If staffing is inadequate, the client is not accepted, or is placed on a documented waiting list with the client's agreement.

The RN schedules and completes the initial in-home assessment (CLN-05). During this visit the RN assesses home suitability (safety hazards, working utilities, sanitation, access, pets, smoking in the home under CLN-07, and any risk to staff under CLN-22) and records the findings.

The RN asks about family and other caregiver availability and willingness to help, and records which tasks are, and are not, provided by family or others. Family availability may inform the plan of care but does not by itself exclude a client who needs services.

The RN and Agency Director review the intake and assessment findings together and decide whether to accept the client. The decision, the date and the names and signatures of the decision-makers are documented in the client record (CLN-12).

If the client is accepted, the Agency Director or Service Supervisor completes admission under CLN-10, provides the rights packet (CLN-01), signs the service agreement (CLN-18), and develops the plan of care (CLN-06).

If the client is not accepted because needs cannot be met, the Service Supervisor notifies the referral source, by phone or in writing, no later than 2 business days after the decision, and states the reason. The Service Supervisor also gives the client or family the names of at least one other agency or resource. Both actions are documented.
Medicaid clients are accepted only with a valid authorization or approved service plan (MED-01, MED-02). Staff start services only for the units and tasks authorized.

Before reducing or ending service for any reason, the Service Supervisor gives the client or representative 48 hours' notice, orally and in writing, unless a listed exception in 10A NCAC 13J .1101 applies. The Agency Director checks the rule text, approves any use of an exception in writing, and records the exception relied on.
When service is reduced or ended, staff help the client transition by referring to other agencies and coordinating with the referral source and any other providers (CLN-03, CLN-10).
If the agency intends to serve clients beyond its stated service area without opening a new site, the Agency Director revises ADM-03 and gives DHSR 30 days' written notice before expanding (SUP-02).
The Agency Director reviews acceptance denials, waiting lists and notices of reduction or ending at the annual program evaluation (ADM-08) to confirm intake criteria are applied consistently.

responsibilities.duty: Makes or approves each acceptance decision, approves use of any 48-hour notice exception, and ensures service area compliance and DHSR notice of expansion.
Assesses the home, client needs and family availability and recommends acceptance or referral.
Confirms staffing and absence coverage, notifies referral sources and clients, and arranges referrals.
Screen for service area and scope, document intake and track staffing capacity.

documentation: Intake Form with screening results
Staffing and absence-coverage determination
RN home suitability and family availability findings
Signed acceptance or non-acceptance decision
Notice to referral source and referral record
Written 48-hour notices of reduction or ending and any exception documentation
Waiting list records
Copies of DHSR notices on service area changes

policies.title: Initial In-Home Assessment (In-Home Aide Services)
policies.applies_to: RN/assessing practitioner, Service Supervisor, Agency Director
policies.purpose: To make sure every in-home aide client is assessed in his or her own home by a qualified health care practitioner before services are planned, so the plan of care meets actual needs.
policies.policy: This policy meets Client Care Policies item .1107(d)(e): Initial Assessment policy (In-Home Aide Services), 10A NCAC 13J .1107(d)-(f). Before a plan of care is written, a health care practitioner, which at [AGENCY NAME] is a Registered Nurse (RN), assesses the client in the client's home. The assessment addresses the client's social, mental, physical, environmental and economic status, and the client's activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). The practitioner signs and dates the assessment. The agency's RN is available for supervision and consultation during all hours in-home aide services are provided, and makes a home visit to develop the plan of care. The initial assessment, goals and client approval are kept in the client record as required by 10A NCAC 13J .1402. For Medicaid clients, the agency's licensure assessment is separate from the Medicaid authorization or assessment (MED-01, MED-02) and does not replace it.

definitions.definition: For this policy, a North Carolina-licensed Registered Nurse employed by or contracted with the agency who has the authority to assess and plan in-home aide care.
Basic self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, eating, transferring and walking.
Tasks that support independent living, such as meal preparation, housekeeping, laundry, shopping, transportation and use of the telephone.
The first in-home visit at which the RN assesses the client and, in the same visit, delivers the client rights packet.

procedures: After intake screening under CLN-04, the Service Supervisor schedules the RN's initial in-home assessment visit at a time convenient for the client and any family. The visit must occur before the plan of care is written and before any aide services begin.
The Agency Director confirms that the RN performing the assessment holds a current NC RN license, verified under PER-01, and has been oriented to the agency's assessment tool.

At the start of the visit, the RN identifies himself or herself and explains the purpose of the visit. The RN delivers the client rights and responsibilities packet, the DHSR hotline notice and complaint contact, and obtains the signed receipt (CLN-01, CLN-02).
The RN assesses the client's social status, including living arrangement, family and other supports, community resources and cultural and language preferences.
The RN assesses mental status, including orientation, memory, mood, judgment and the client's ability to direct his or her own care.

The RN assesses physical status, including diagnoses, medications (without directing aides to perform tasks outside CLN-13), mobility, balance and fall risk, skin condition, continence, nutrition, sensory deficits and pain.

The RN assesses the home environment, including safety hazards, cleanliness, utilities, equipment, pets, firearms, smoking (CLN-07), and the safety of the home for staff (CLN-22), and records home suitability findings for the acceptance decision (CLN-04).

The RN assesses economic status as it affects care, including payer source, ability to pay, and eligibility for Medicaid or other programs, and refers the client for benefits screening when appropriate (CLN-03).
The RN assesses the client's ability to perform each ADL and IADL, notes the level of assistance required for each, and identifies tasks the client and family can do or will do.
The RN discusses the client's preferences, needs and goals with the client and family, and records them in the client's own terms where possible.

The RN completes the written assessment form, and signs and dates it on the day of the visit. The RN adds his or her title and license number. An unsigned or undated assessment is not valid and cannot support a plan of care.
The RN uses the assessment to write the plan of care with the client's participation (CLN-06). Client approval of the goals and plan is documented in the record (10A NCAC 13J .1402).
The RN files the signed assessment in the client record within 2 business days (CLN-12) and gives the Service Supervisor the information needed to assign an aide and set the schedule.

For Medicaid PCS and CAP/DA clients, the RN reviews the Medicaid assessment or authorization, reconciles it with the agency's assessment, and reports any differences or unmet needs to the authorization source as described in MED-01 and MED-02.

The RN is available for supervision and consultation during all hours aide services are provided. The Agency Director publishes an RN on-call schedule, with phone numbers, to aides and clients (CLN-08, ADM-02).
The RN performs a new in-home assessment, or an updated one, when the client's condition changes significantly (CLN-20) and during the 90-day review (CLN-06). Each new assessment is signed and dated.

The Agency Director audits a sample of client records each quarter to verify that every initial assessment is complete, signed, dated and done before the plan of care and before services started, and reports results at the program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Performs the in-home assessment before the plan of care, covers all required domains, signs and dates it, and is available for supervision and consultation.
Verifies RN licensure and availability, publishes the on-call schedule and audits assessment records.
Schedules the assessment visit, assigns aides based on the assessment and files the record.
Work only from the plan of care built on the assessment and report changes to the supervisor or RN.

documentation: Signed and dated initial in-home assessment covering social, mental, physical, environmental and economic status, ADLs and IADLs
RN credential verification
Client rights receipt signed at the initial evaluation visit
Documentation of client goals and client approval of the plan
RN on-call/availability schedule
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Plan of Care Development, Orders and 90-Day Review
policies.applies_to: All in-home aide clients (private pay, Medicaid State Plan PCS and CAP/DA); Registered Nurse/health care practitioner, Service Supervisor, caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure every in-home aide service and item is delivered under a written plan of care that is built with the client, signed, kept in the home, ordered when an order is required, and reviewed at least every 90 days.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides no in-home aide service until a plan of care specifies the services and items to be provided. The plan is built with the client (and the client's representative, if any) and is signed by the health care practitioner and the client. A copy is kept in the client's home. The plan states the type of service, frequency and duration, restrictions, safety measures and goals, and the level of assistance the client needs for each activity of daily living (ADL). The practitioner reviews the plan at least every 90 days. When an order for in-home aide services is required, a prescriber signs it and the original is placed in the client record. Care may begin on a verbal order in the interim. When physician orders are required, the physician is notified of changes to the plan. This policy meets Client Care Policies: .1202(a-b) / .1107(a)(b) (Plan of care policy, including 90-day review; In-Home Aide Services) and checklist item A(4), development of, and updates to, the plan of care, under 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(4). For Medicaid CAP/DA clients, the plan is person-centered and consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c) and the care plan from the case management entity (see MED-02).

definitions.definition: The written document that specifies the services and items to be provided to a client, including service type, frequency, duration, restrictions, safety measures, goals and assistance level per ADL.
The Registered Nurse or other qualified licensed practitioner designated by the agency to develop, sign and review the plan of care and to supervise aides.
The degree of help the client needs with each ADL (for example, supervision/cueing, limited assistance or extensive assistance), recorded separately for each ADL.
The physician or other practitioner authorized under North Carolina law to sign orders for the services.
An order given orally by a prescriber that allows care to begin on an interim basis until the signed order is received.

procedures: The Intake Coordinator confirms during the accept/decline decision (CLN-04) whether an order is required for the requested service, based on the payer and program (private pay, State Plan PCS, CAP/DA), and records the answer on the intake form.

The practitioner (RN) makes the in-home assessment visit (CLN-05) before or on the day services start and uses it to build the plan of care with the client and, with the client's permission, the family or representative.
The practitioner records on the plan the type of service, frequency, duration, restrictions, safety measures and measurable goals, in plain language the client can understand.

The practitioner enters the assistance level for each ADL (bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, mobility/transfers, grooming, and any others to be performed) and lists any household or other tasks the aide will perform.
The practitioner lists tasks the aide will not perform and any client-specific restrictions or precautions (for example, fall risk, diet limits, mobility devices).

The practitioner reviews the plan with the client, explains it, and answers questions. The client signs and dates the plan to show approval, and the practitioner signs and dates it. The Service Supervisor does not sign in place of the practitioner.

If an order is required, the Service Supervisor requests it from the prescriber before the first visit. If the signed order has not arrived, the practitioner may take a verbal order, write it in the record with date, time, prescriber name and the practitioner's signature, and care may begin on that basis.

The Service Supervisor follows up on every verbal order and obtains the prescriber's signature. When the signed order is received, the original is placed in the client record. The Service Supervisor escalates to the Administrator any signed order still outstanding after 14 days.

For Medicaid clients, the Service Supervisor confirms that the plan of care matches the authorization and service plan (MED-01) and, for CAP/DA, the CAP/DA care plan (MED-02). Services in excess of the authorization are not scheduled.
The Service Supervisor places a copy of the signed plan in the client's home on or before the first visit and records the date it was placed. The original stays in the client record.

The Service Supervisor gives the plan to each assigned caregiver before the caregiver's first visit and reviews it with the caregiver. The caregiver signs that they have read it. Caregivers are assigned only to tasks they have demonstrated to the practitioner (see CLN-08, PER-02).

The practitioner reviews the plan with the client at least every 90 days, as part of the 90-day review (ADM-09) and supervisory visit (CLN-08). The review covers whether goals are met, whether assistance levels and hours still fit, and whether any safety issue has arisen. The practitioner signs and dates the review.

The practitioner revises the plan whenever the client's condition, needs, or service request changes (CLN-20), and does not wait for the 90-day date. The client signs the revised plan, and the revised copy replaces the old copy in the home on the same day or the next scheduled visit.
When physician orders are required, the practitioner notifies the physician of changes to the plan, and obtains a new or updated order. The notice, date and response are documented in the record.
Caregivers report any change in the client's condition or any problem with the plan to the Service Supervisor the same day (CLN-13, CLN-20). The Service Supervisor notifies the practitioner promptly.

The Administrator audits a sample of records at least quarterly to check that each plan is signed by the client and practitioner, includes all required content, is in the home, has an order if one is required, and has been reviewed within 90 days. Findings go into the annual evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Assess, build, sign, review (at least every 90 days) and revise the plan of care; take and follow up on verbal orders; notify the physician of changes when orders are required.
Obtain orders, place the copy in the home, distribute the plan to caregivers, track 90-day due dates, and ensure the plan matches the payer authorization.
Follow the plan exactly, perform only tasks listed on it, and report changes or problems the same day.
Maintain this policy, audit records quarterly, and correct deficiencies.
Take part in developing the plan, sign it, and tell the agency when needs change.

documentation: Signed and dated plan of care (client and practitioner signatures) in the client record
Copy of the plan in the client's home with date placed
Original signed prescriber order and verbal order entries with follow-up dates
90-day review entries and revised plans
Physician notification of changes (date, content, response)
Caregiver acknowledgement of the plan
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: No Smoking in Client Homes
policies.applies_to: All employees and contractors providing services in client homes; Intake Coordinator, Service Supervisor, Administrator
policies.purpose: To comply with North Carolina law that prohibits agency employees and contractors from smoking while providing services in a client's home, and to make sure clients are told of the prohibition.
policies.policy: No employee or contractor of [AGENCY NAME] may smoke while providing services in a client's home. The agency tells each client of this prohibition at intake, and each staff member signs an acknowledgment at orientation. An administrative penalty of up to $200 per violation may be assessed under the statute. Violations are handled under the agency's corrective-action process. This policy meets Client Care Policies: G.S. 131E-143, the No Smoking policy.

definitions.definition: Lighting or using a cigarette, cigar, pipe or other tobacco product, in the home. For this policy the agency also treats the use of electronic cigarettes and vaping devices as prohibited during visits.
From arrival at the client's home until departure, including paid breaks taken in the home and time on the premises or at the entrance.
Any individual or agency that provides services in client homes under an arrangement with [AGENCY NAME] (see CLN-09).

procedures: The Administrator posts this policy in the personnel handbook and includes it in the orientation curriculum (PER-06).
At orientation, before any client contact, each new employee reads the policy and signs and dates a No Smoking Acknowledgment. The signed form is placed in the personnel record.

Contractor agreements (CLN-09) include a clause that contractor staff may not smoke in client homes. The Service Supervisor confirms that contractor staff have signed the acknowledgment before they are assigned.

At intake, the Intake Coordinator tells the client and family of the prohibition, explains that it applies to all staff and contractors, and records the date and the client's response on the intake form. The prohibition is also stated in the client service agreement (CLN-18).

Caregivers do not smoke in the home, on the property at the client's entrance, or in view of the client while on duty. A caregiver who needs to smoke may do so only on an unpaid break away from the client's home and out of sight of the client, and must not leave the client unattended to do so.
Caregivers do not ask clients or visitors for ignition sources or tobacco products, and do not accept them as gifts (CLN-16).

Caregivers do not light a client's cigarette or assist with smoking in a way that places the caregiver in violation of this policy. If a client smokes during a visit and the client's smoking creates a safety risk (for example, oxygen in use, impaired alertness, fire risk), the caregiver moves away from danger and calls the Service Supervisor at once, and the matter is recorded as an incident if applicable (CLN-15, CLN-22).
The Service Supervisor asks clients and families, at supervisory visits, whether any staff member has smoked or smelled of smoke in the home.
Any client, family member or staff member may report a suspected violation to the Service Supervisor or Administrator at [PHONE]. Reports are accepted without retaliation (CLN-02).
The Administrator investigates each report within two business days by interviewing the client, caregiver and Service Supervisor, and records the findings.

If a violation is confirmed, the Administrator applies progressive discipline (written warning for the first violation; further discipline up to termination for repeat violations), records the action in the personnel record, and notifies the client of the outcome.
The Administrator tracks any administrative penalty assessed and the reason, and reports the count of substantiated violations in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the policy, ensure acknowledgments are signed, investigate reports and apply corrective action.
Tell each client of the prohibition at intake and document it.
Check compliance at supervisory visits and verify contractor acknowledgments.
Do not smoke while providing services in a client's home; report concerns.

documentation: Signed No Smoking Acknowledgment in each personnel record
Intake form entry showing the client was informed
Client service agreement provision
Contractor agreement clause and acknowledgments
Complaint/violation investigation and corrective-action records

policies.title: Supervision of Staff and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: RN/health care practitioner, Service Supervisor, all in-home aides; companion, sitter and respite staff if the agency offers those services
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers are supervised by a qualified practitioner, assigned only tasks they have shown they can do, and observed in the home at the required intervals.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supervises all personnel who give care. The health care practitioner makes a supervisory visit to each client's home at least every 90 days, whether or not the caregiver is present, and also visits at least annually while the caregiver is providing care. Each visit is recorded with the date, findings and signature, and any corrective action is documented. The practitioner is available during all hours services are provided. Caregivers are assigned only tasks they have demonstrated to the health care practitioner, and the demonstration is documented. Supervision may be delegated to the Service Supervisor under this policy only if the practitioner stays available and accountable. If the agency provides companion, sitter or respite services, staff are supervised by contacting the client at least every 3 months and visiting the home at least every 6 months, and a visit is also made annually while the aide is in the home. This policy meets Client Care Policies: .1001(a)(3); .1110(c-g); .1504(2) (Supervision of Staff; Companion Sitters .1504(2)) and checklist item A(3), supervision of personnel, 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(3).

definitions.definition: An in-home visit by the practitioner (or delegate as described in this policy) to review the client's condition, the plan of care and the caregiver's performance.
Supervision assigned by this policy to another qualified person, permitted only when the practitioner remains available and accountable for it.
Non-hands-on staff providing companion, sitter or respite services only (see ADM-05).
Retraining, counseling, reassignment or other steps taken to resolve a deficiency found during supervision.

procedures: The Administrator designates the supervising practitioner(s) and the Service Supervisor in writing (ADM-06) and records the supervision structure on the organization chart (SUP-01).

If any supervisory tasks are delegated to the Service Supervisor, the Administrator writes the delegation, naming the tasks and the practitioner who remains accountable. The practitioner stays reachable during every service hour, and the on-call number is given to caregivers and clients ([PHONE]).

Before assigning any task, the practitioner observes the caregiver demonstrate it, or reviews a documented demonstration, and records the tasks and date on the Competency Record (PER-02). The Service Supervisor assigns only tasks listed as demonstrated.
At each client's start of care, the Service Supervisor enters in the client record the date on which the 90-day visit and annual visit will fall due, and tracks them on the supervision log.

The practitioner makes a supervisory visit to every in-home aide client at least every 90 days, regardless of whether the caregiver is present. The practitioner reviews the plan of care (CLN-06), the client's condition and satisfaction, and the home environment.

At least once a year while the caregiver is providing care, the practitioner visits while the caregiver is present and observes the caregiver's work against the plan of care. The visit is scheduled so that no caregiver or client goes more than 12 months without an observed visit.
At each visit the practitioner records the date, findings and signature on the Supervisory Visit Form and places it in the client record.

When the practitioner finds a deficiency (for example, a task done incorrectly, a plan not followed, a safety hazard), the practitioner records the corrective action, who will carry it out and by when, and follows up and records the result. The deficiency is also noted in the caregiver's personnel record.
If a visit reveals a change in the client's condition, the practitioner revises the plan of care and informs the physician if orders are required (CLN-06, CLN-20).

For companion, sitter or respite services, if offered, the Service Supervisor contacts each client at least every 3 months and visits the home at least every 6 months, and makes an additional visit annually while the aide is in the home. Each contact and visit is documented with date, findings and signature. A supervisor is available on-site when necessary.

The Service Supervisor runs the supervision log weekly and notifies the Administrator of any visit due within 14 days. A visit that falls overdue is reported to the Administrator the same day and is completed within 3 business days.
The Administrator reviews the supervision log monthly and reports the on-time rate in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Make supervisory visits, verify task demonstrations, stay available during service hours, and stay accountable for any delegated supervision.
Track due dates, assign only demonstrated tasks, make non-hands-on staff contacts and visits, and follow through on corrective action.
Designate supervisors, approve any delegation in writing, review the supervision log monthly.
Perform only demonstrated tasks, take part in visits and complete corrective action.

documentation: Supervisory Visit Forms (date, findings, signature)
Corrective-action records and follow-up
Task demonstration records (PER-02)
Supervision log
Written delegation of supervision
Companion/sitter 3-month contacts and 6-month visits, if applicable

policies.title: Arrangements for Services with Other Agencies or Individuals
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Service Supervisor; any agency, individual or contractor providing services on behalf of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure any services delivered through another agency or individual are covered by a signed written agreement and meet the same standards as services given by agency employees.
policies.policy: When [AGENCY NAME] arranges for services to be provided by another agency or an individual, it uses a signed written agreement that contains the terms required by 10A NCAC 13J .1111, including the services to be provided, the term of the agreement, fees, verification of licensure, supervision, equal personnel standards, documentation, and the geographic area. The agency verifies the contractor's licensure, applies the same personnel standards as for its own employees, and keeps ultimate responsibility for contracted services. Each agreement is reviewed annually. This policy meets Client Care Policies: .1111(a-d), the Arrangements for Services with other Agencies or Individuals policy.

definitions.definition: A service the agency has agreed to provide that is carried out by another agency or an individual who is not an agency employee.
Contractor personnel meet the same qualifications, checks, competency, registry and training requirements as agency employees.
The agency remains responsible to the client, to payers and to DHSR for the quality and safety of contracted services.

procedures: Before any contract is signed, the Administrator decides whether a contracted arrangement is needed and records the reason (for example, a service outside the agency's staff capacity) and confirms the service and area fall within the agency's scope and geographic area (ADM-01, ADM-03).

The Administrator verifies that the contractor holds any license required for the service and records the license number, status and date checked. If the contractor is an individual, the Administrator verifies the individual's professional or registry credentials, as applicable (PER-01).

The Administrator verifies that contractor personnel who will enter client homes have the same background check, Health Care Personnel Registry check, Nurse Aide Registry status (where required), TB screening, competency verification and training as agency employees (PER-01, PER-02, PER-07, ADM-12). The agency does not use any contractor personnel with a substantiated HCPR finding (CLN-11).

The Administrator prepares the written agreement using the agency's Contract Template, which includes each term required by .1111: services to be provided, term of the agreement, fees, verification of licensure, supervision, equal personnel standards, documentation to be furnished to the agency, geographic area, and the remaining terms listed on the Contract Checklist.
The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] retains ultimate responsibility for contracted services, directs the plan of care, and supervises the services through its practitioner (CLN-08).

The agreement requires the contractor to document each service in a form the agency can place in the client record, and to give the agency that documentation by the date stated in the agreement (CLN-12).

The agreement requires the contractor to follow the agency's policies on client rights, confidentiality, abuse/neglect reporting, incident reporting and no smoking (CLN-01, ADM-15, CLN-14, CLN-15, CLN-07), and to report incidents to the agency the same day.
Both parties sign and date the agreement before the contractor serves any client. The Administrator files the signed agreement in the contract file and keeps a contract log.
The Service Supervisor includes any contracted service in the client's plan of care and makes sure the client knows who will provide the service.
The Service Supervisor and practitioner supervise contractor staff in the same manner and at the same intervals as agency employees (CLN-08), and record findings.

The Administrator reviews each agreement at least annually, confirms licensure and personnel verification are current, and records the review date, any change and signature. An agreement not reviewed in 12 months is suspended until the review is done.

The Administrator reports contracted service volume, complaints and any concerns in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08). If the contractor fails to meet standards, the Administrator ends the arrangement, arranges replacement services so the client does not lose care (CLN-19), and documents the action.

responsibilities.duty: Approve, sign, verify, review annually and, if needed, terminate contractor arrangements; retain ultimate responsibility.
Coordinate contracted services in the plan of care, receive contractor documentation and supervise contractor staff.
Meet licensure, personnel and documentation terms and follow agency policies.

documentation: Signed written agreement for each contractor
Licensure verification record
Personnel verification records for contractor staff
Contract log and annual review record
Contractor service documentation in the client record
Supervision records for contractor staff

policies.title: Admission, Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Intake Coordinator, RN/health care practitioner, Service Supervisor, Administrator; all clients
policies.purpose: To set out when [AGENCY NAME] admits clients, how it gives notice and discharges, transfers or reduces service, and how it records and learns from discharges.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits only clients whose needs it can safely meet within its scope of services and geographic area (CLN-04). The agency gives the client at least 48 hours' notice before reducing or ending service, except where an exception listed in 10A NCAC 13J .1101 applies. A discharge summary is completed for every client and placed in the client record, and the agency refers the client to other providers and documents the coordination. Discharge reasons are analyzed in the annual program evaluation. This policy meets Client Care Policies: .1001(a)(2) & .1402(2)(d), Discharge policy, and checklist item A(2), admission and discharge policies, 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(2).

definitions.definition: The date the agency accepts the client, the signed service agreement and plan of care are in place and the first service is provided.
Ending all services because goals are met, the client or representative requests it, the client moves, the agency can no longer meet the client's needs, or another reason described in this policy.
Moving the client's services to another provider, with the client's consent and with records sent as authorized.
The agency ending or reducing any service or hours, whether or not the client is fully discharged.
A written summary in the client record, listing dates of service, services provided, reason for discharge, client status and referrals made.

procedures: Admission: the Intake Coordinator takes the referral, records the referral source and applies the acceptance criteria in CLN-04, including adequate staff and coverage for absences, suitability of the home, family or other support availability, and whether the service and location are within the agency's scope and area.

The RN completes the in-home assessment (CLN-05) and the plan of care (CLN-06). Admission is complete when the client signs the service agreement (CLN-18) and the rights form (CLN-01), and the record contains admission data required by the record policy (CLN-12).

If the agency cannot meet the client's needs, the Intake Coordinator tells the referral source and the client promptly, gives the reason, refers the client to other agencies able to serve, and records the date and result.

Reduction or discontinuation: before reducing or ending any service, the Service Supervisor or Administrator discusses it with the client and gives written notice at least 48 hours in advance, recording the date, time and method of notice. Where the client agreed to the change and signs the notice, the signature is recorded.

Where a listed exception in 10A NCAC 13J .1101 applies and shorter notice is given, the Administrator records the specific exception relied on and the facts, and informs the client in writing as soon as possible.

For Medicaid PCS and CAP/DA clients, the Administrator also follows the Medicaid notice and case management coordination requirements (MED-01, MED-02), and notifies the case manager of any reduction or discharge.

Transfer: with the client's written authorization, the Service Supervisor sends the receiving provider the information needed for continuity of care (current plan of care, recent assessment, current medications list noted in the record, and the discharge summary), and records what was sent, when and to whom (ADM-15).

Referral: the Service Supervisor gives the client or family the names of other available providers or community resources (CLN-03) and records them. The agency continues services through the notice period unless a listed exception applies, so the client is not left without care.
If the client dies, the Service Supervisor notes the date and circumstances, notifies the practitioner and Administrator, and completes a closing entry within 5 business days.

Within 7 days after the last service, the RN or Service Supervisor completes the discharge summary (dates of service, services given, client status at discharge, reason for discharge, referrals and coordination) and signs and dates it.
The Service Supervisor collects the plan of care copy and any agency items from the home, if the client agrees, and records the return.
The Administrator reviews each discharge within 5 business days and, where discharge arose from a complaint or incident, confirms follow-up (CLN-02, CLN-15).
The record is closed and retained according to CLN-12.
The Administrator tallies discharges by reason each quarter and reports the findings in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Apply acceptance criteria, notify referral sources, and refer clients the agency cannot serve.
Assess, decide on clinical discharge, sign the discharge summary and coordinate transfers.
Give notices, coordinate referral and transfer, close the record.
Approve discharges for agency-initiated reasons, apply exceptions, analyze discharge reasons.

documentation: Intake form and referral source record
48-hour notice record (date, time, method, any exception)
Discharge summary
Referral and coordination notes
Transfer authorization and records-sent log
Quarterly discharge-reason tally

policies.title: Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR) Reporting
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Service Supervisor, RN, all employees and contractors
policies.purpose: To make sure allegations against health care personnel are reported to the NC Health Care Personnel Registry, investigated and documented, and that the agency never hires anyone with a substantiated registry finding.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports allegations against health care personnel to the DHSR Health Care Personnel Registry, including abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation of client property, as required by 10A NCAC 13O .0102. The agency does not hire, directly or by contract, anyone with a substantiated finding on the Registry (10A NCAC 13J .1003(c)). Each report and the investigation are documented. This policy meets Client Care Policies: 10A NCAC 13O .0102, Health Care Personnel Registry reporting policy. The Administrator confirms the current text of that rule, including the report time frame and form, at each annual policy review (ADM-16), and the agency's reporting deadlines in this policy are never longer than the rule allows.

definitions.definition: The DHSR registry of health care personnel with substantiated findings of abuse, neglect, exploitation, misappropriation of property or other listed conduct.
A report or reasonable suspicion, from any source, that a staff member or contractor has committed an act covered by the rule.
A finding entered on the HCPR after DHSR's review. A person with a substantiated finding may not be hired by the agency.
Taking or using a client's property or funds without consent or authority.

procedures: Any employee or contractor who sees, learns of or suspects abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation involving agency personnel reports it immediately to the Service Supervisor or Administrator, and the same day in writing. If both are unreachable, the employee calls [PHONE] for the on-call line.

If a client is in danger, the caregiver or supervisor first protects the client: calls 911 if necessary, makes sure the client is safe, and removes the accused from client contact pending review (CLN-14).
The supervisor tells the Administrator the same business day, and the Administrator opens a case file with the date, time, source, client, staff member involved and the allegation.

The Administrator decides whether the allegation falls within the reporting criteria of 10A NCAC 13O .0102, using the rule text kept in the policy binder. If there is doubt, the Administrator reports.

The Administrator makes the report to the HCPR, DHSR (919-855-3968), within the time frame set by 10A NCAC 13O .0102, on the form DHSR requires, and records the date, time, method, name of the person reporting and any confirmation received.

Where the allegation also involves abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client, the Administrator makes any separate report required to adult protective services, law enforcement or other authorities (CLN-14) and records it.

The Administrator starts an internal investigation promptly: interviewing the client (with care for the client's comfort and rights), the accused, witnesses and other staff, reviewing visit records, EVV data (MED-03) and the plan of care, and obtaining written statements.
The accused is kept from client contact while the investigation runs. The agency arranges replacement care so the client is not left without services (CLN-19).
The Administrator completes the investigation and submits any written follow-up or investigation findings to the HCPR, within the time DHSR requires, and records the date submitted.
The Administrator informs the client or representative of the outcome of the agency's investigation, to the extent allowed by confidentiality law (ADM-15), and documents the notice.
If the allegation is confirmed, the Administrator applies disciplinary action up to termination, records it in the personnel record, and cooperates with DHSR.

Before hiring any employee or accepting any contractor, and as part of annual verification, the Administrator checks the HCPR and records the result and date in the personnel record (PER-07). The agency does not hire, directly or by contract, anyone with a substantiated finding.
If the Administrator learns that a current employee has a substantiated finding, the agency removes the employee from client contact the same day and ends employment.
Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited (CLN-02).

The Administrator logs every HCPR report and outcome and reviews the log in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08). Training on this policy is part of orientation and annual in-service (PER-06, PER-05).

responsibilities.duty: Decide on and make HCPR reports, lead investigations, check the HCPR before hire, and keep the HCPR log.
Receive reports, protect the client, preserve evidence, and escalate the same day.
Assess any client harm and assist in the investigation.
Report allegations immediately and cooperate with investigations.

documentation: Allegation intake and case file
HCPR report with confirmation of the date and method
Investigation notes, statements and findings
Replacement-care arrangements
Disciplinary action
HCPR check results in personnel records
HCPR report log

policies.title: Client Record Content, Handling and Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Service Supervisor/RN, scheduler, office staff and all in-home aides and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, accurate, secure and retrievable service record for every client. The record documents the care given and the client's approval of it, and it is available to DHSR surveyors and to authorized staff.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] keeps a written service record for every client, in accordance with 10A NCAC 13J .1401 and .1402. This policy meets the checklist item 'Client Care Policies: .1401(a-f) & .1402(a)(b) – Client record content & handling' and checklist item A(6), 'time frame for completion and return of service records to the agency' (10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(6)).

(1) Record handling (.1401). The client's name appears on every page of the record. Every entry carries the true date on which it was written. An entry written after the date of service is labeled 'late entry' and shows both the date written and the date of service. Original records stay secure on the agency premises at [ADDRESS]. A record that is removed from the premises must be returned within 5 working days, and every removal is logged on a sign-out log. Records are kept for 5 years after the client is discharged. For a client who is a minor, records are kept until 3 years after the client turns 18.

(2) Record content (.1402). The admission portion contains identification of the client, the signed client rights form, next of kin or emergency contact, referral source, and the home assessment. The service portion contains the initial assessment, the goals of service, evidence of the client's approval of the plan, dated and signed service entries, a discharge summary, and evidence of coordination with other providers or agencies.

(3) Time frame for completion and return of service records (checklist item A(6)). Caregivers complete their service entries for each visit before leaving the home or, at the latest, before the end of that shift. Paper service records and timesheets are returned to the agency within 7 calendar days of the end of each pay period and, in all cases, before the monthly record review. Electronic entries are completed at the time of service. Any record, entry or signature not received by the due date is treated as delinquent. The Service Supervisor follows it up the next business day.

(4) Privacy and security. Client records are protected under CLN-... and ADM-15 and the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530. Access is limited to staff who need the information to do their jobs.

definitions.definition: The agency's complete written or electronic file for a client, containing the admission data and service data required by 10A NCAC 13J .1402.
An entry made after the day on which the service or event occurred. It is labeled 'late entry' and shows both the current date and the date of the service or event.
A written log recording who removed an original record, the client name, the date removed, the reason, and the date returned.
Monday through Friday, excluding state and federal holidays.

procedures: At referral, the Intake Coordinator opens a record for the client and records the client's identification, referral source and next of kin or emergency contact on the admission data sheet the same day.

The Service Supervisor/RN obtains the client's signature on the client rights form (CLN-01) at or before the first service and files it in the admission section. The date is entered by the person signing.
The RN files the home assessment (CLN-05) and the initial assessment in the record within 2 business days of the visit.
The Service Supervisor files the plan of care, the service goals, and evidence of the client's approval (signature or documented verbal approval) within 2 business days of completion (CLN-06).
Staff write the client's full name on every page of the record, paper or electronic, including each page of attachments, faxes and scanned documents.
Caregivers complete each dated, signed service entry at the time of the visit. Each entry shows the tasks performed, the time in and time out, and any change in condition or incident.

Staff use the true date on every entry. Staff never backdate, pre-date or overwrite. A correction is made with one line through the error, with the writer's initials, date and the word 'error', so the original entry stays legible.
A person who enters information after the date of service marks it 'late entry', shows the date and time written and the date of service, and signs it.
Caregivers return all paper service records and timesheets to the agency within 7 calendar days after the end of each pay period. The scheduler logs their receipt.

The Service Supervisor reviews returned entries for completeness within 3 business days of receipt. Where an entry is missing, the supervisor requests completion from the caregiver in writing and follows up until the entry is made as a labeled late entry.

The Service Supervisor reports to the Administrator any caregiver whose records are repeatedly late or incomplete. Late records are addressed through the performance process (PER-04) and may affect scheduling.
The Administrator keeps original records in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system on the agency premises at [ADDRESS]. Only authorized staff have keys or log-in access.
A staff member who needs to remove an original record from the premises must obtain the Service Supervisor's approval and complete the sign-out log before the record leaves the premises.

The Service Supervisor reviews the sign-out log weekly. The record must be returned within 5 working days. The Administrator is told about any overdue record on the 6th working day, and the record is retrieved.
A copy of the plan of care is kept in the client's home (CLN-06). Home copies are not substitutes for the original in the agency record.
The Service Supervisor completes a discharge summary and files it in the record when services end (CLN-10).

The office staff mark the date of discharge on the record cover and move the record to closed storage. The destruction date is set at 5 years after discharge. For a minor, it is set at 3 years after the client's 18th birthday.

Before destroying any record, the Administrator confirms the retention period has passed and that there is no pending investigation, audit, complaint or legal hold. The Administrator documents the destruction by signing a destruction log. Records are shredded or electronically purged so that they cannot be reconstructed.
The Administrator provides surveyors immediate access to records on request (SUP-02). Staff do not release records to anyone else without client authorization or legal authority (ADM-15).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures secure storage, the sign-out log, retention and destruction practices, and surveyor access to records.
Maintains admission and service data, reviews returned entries, follows up on late or missing records, and writes the discharge summary.
Opens records, logs returned timesheets, manages the sign-out log and closed-file storage.
Complete accurate, dated and signed service entries at each visit, label late entries, and return records within the stated time frame.

documentation: Client service record (admission data and service data)
Record sign-out log
Delinquent record follow-up notes
Record destruction log
Timesheet and service record receipt log

policies.title: Caregiver Permitted Duties and Medication Assistance
policies.applies_to: Service Supervisor/RN, scheduler, in-home aides and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers perform only the tasks that are listed in the client's plan of care and that they have been shown to perform competently. It also sets clear limits on medication assistance so that aides assist with, but never administer, medications.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] assigns caregivers only tasks that (1) are listed in the client's current plan of care, signed by the health care practitioner and the client (10A NCAC 13J .1107), and (2) the caregiver has demonstrated to the health care practitioner, with the demonstration documented and kept on file (10A NCAC 13J .1110). Terms used in this policy have the meanings given in 10A NCAC 13J .0901, including activities of daily living (ADLs), instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), extensive and limited assistance, and hands-on care.

Aides may assist the client with self-administration of ordered medications. Medication reminders are an IADL under 10A NCAC 13J .0901. Aides may not administer medications. Caregivers who give extensive assistance with an ADL must be listed on the NC Nurse Aide Registry (see PER-01). Aides must report changes in a client's condition to the supervisor. Supervision of caregivers may be delegated by this policy to a qualified Service Supervisor only if the health care practitioner remains available and accountable (CLN-08). The plan of care states the level of assistance for each ADL.

definitions.definition: Basic self-care activities such as bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, mobility and transferring, as defined in 10A NCAC 13J .0901.
Activities such as meal preparation, housekeeping, shopping, laundry and medication reminders, as defined in 10A NCAC 13J .0901.
The levels of hands-on help a client needs with an ADL, as defined in 10A NCAC 13J .0901. The plan of care states the level for each ADL.

Reminding the client to take a medication ordered by a practitioner and helping the client who is taking his or her own medication, for example by handing over the container the client has identified as his or hers. The client, not the aide, takes the medication.
Selecting, preparing, measuring, giving or otherwise directing the taking of a medication for a client who cannot do so. This is outside the scope of aide duties at [AGENCY NAME].
As defined in 10A NCAC 13J .0901 by reference to G.S. 90-640(a).

procedures: The Service Supervisor/RN lists each task the caregiver will perform, with the level of assistance for each ADL, on the plan of care. The health care practitioner and the client sign it (CLN-06).
The Service Supervisor places a copy of the signed plan of care in the client's home before the first aide visit and files the original in the agency record.

The scheduler checks the caregiver's task-competency record before assigning a caregiver to a client. The scheduler assigns only caregivers whose record shows each task on that client's plan as demonstrated.

Before first performing a task, the caregiver demonstrates it to the health care practitioner (RN) (PER-02). The RN documents the date, task, outcome and signature, and this record is kept in the personnel file.

For a task the caregiver has not demonstrated, the Service Supervisor/RN arranges the demonstration and observation first. The caregiver does not perform the task in the meantime. If no other qualified caregiver is available, the Service Supervisor informs the client and follows CLN-19.

Before assigning a caregiver to a client who needs extensive assistance with any ADL, the Administrator verifies the caregiver's listing on the Nurse Aide Registry with no substantiated findings and records the verification date (PER-01).

Caregivers do not perform tasks that are not on the plan of care, even if the client or family asks. The caregiver refers the request to the Service Supervisor, who decides whether the plan of care needs to be changed and obtains a signed plan-of-care update before the new task is performed.

Medication assistance may be provided only for medications ordered by a licensed prescriber and listed on the client's plan of care or medication list. The aide does not assist with a medication that is not on the list. The aide calls the supervisor instead.

Aides may provide verbal reminders, may remind a client of the time a medication is due, may open containers at the client's direction, and may hand the client the container the client identifies. The client places the medication in his or her own mouth.

Aides do not select a medication, set up or fill pill organizers, measure a dose, break or crush a medication, change a dose or schedule, give injections or insulin, apply prescription treatments other than as listed on the plan of care and within a task previously demonstrated, or give any medication by any route to a client who cannot take it for himself or herself.

If the client cannot take his or her own medication, refuses it or appears confused about it, the aide does not give it. The aide documents what happened and calls the supervisor right away, who decides on follow-up with the client, the practitioner or the family.

The aide records each medication reminder or assistance on the service entry with the date, time, medication named by the client and the client's response. The aide reports missed doses, refusals, suspected errors and adverse reactions to the supervisor immediately. A suspected medication problem is also documented on an incident report (CLN-15).

The aide reports any change in the client's condition to the supervisor the same day, or immediately if it is urgent. For an emergency, the aide calls 911 first (ADM-02). The supervisor reviews, notifies the practitioner as needed and updates the plan of care (CLN-20).

If supervision of caregivers is delegated to a Service Supervisor under agency policy, the health care practitioner remains available to the Service Supervisor and accountable for the supervision. The agency's delegation is documented in the Service Supervisor's job description (ADM-06).
The Service Supervisor observes the aide in the home at the supervisory visit and checks that only the tasks on the plan of care are being performed in the way they were demonstrated (CLN-08).

The Administrator investigates any caregiver who performs an unauthorized task or administers a medication, removes the caregiver from the assignment pending review and applies corrective action under PER-09. If the client was harmed, the Administrator reviews the case for HCPR reporting (CLN-11).

responsibilities.duty: Writes the plan of care, demonstrates and documents caregiver competency, supervises tasks and medication assistance, and responds to reported changes in condition.
Signs the plan of care, observes caregiver demonstrations and remains available and accountable when supervision is delegated.
Assigns only caregivers with documented competency and required Nurse Aide Registry listing.
Verifies registry listings, investigates scope-of-duty violations and takes corrective action.
Perform only the tasks on the plan of care, assist but never administer medications, and report changes in condition to the supervisor.

documentation: Signed plan of care with level of assistance per ADL
Caregiver task competency/demonstration record
Nurse Aide Registry verification record
Service entries showing tasks and medication reminders
Incident reports for medication concerns
Supervisory visit records

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and supervisors
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation, to ensure that every suspected incident is promptly reported to the right authorities, and to ensure that clients are protected while an allegation is investigated.
policies.policy:
Every [AGENCY NAME] client has the right to be free from abuse, neglect and exploitation (G.S. 131E-144.3). The agency has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect or exploitation by staff, family, or anyone else. This applies to clients receiving private-pay services and Medicaid services, including CAP/DA, where it also supports the person-centered and rights protections for home and community-based services in 42 CFR 441.301(c).

Any employee who suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client must report it to the Administrator immediately. Under North Carolina law, a suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a disabled or older adult is also reported to the county Department of Social Services (DSS) Adult Protective Services in the county where the client lives. The law requires a report by anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services. It does not set a number of hours, so the agency's standard is to report immediately and no later than the end of the same shift. Staff members make the report personally; they do not wait for supervisor approval. The report to the Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR) is made as described in CLN-11. The agency does not hire anyone with a substantiated finding on the HCPR, directly or by contract (10A NCAC 13J .1003(c)). DHSR starts investigations of abuse allegations within 24 hours and neglect within 48 hours (G.S. 131E-144.6), and the agency cooperates fully. The agency investigates any client or family complaint within 72 hours and documents it and its resolution (G.S. 131E-144.6). No one who reports in good faith will be retaliated against.

definitions.definition: The willful infliction of physical pain, injury, mental anguish, unreasonable confinement, or the willful deprivation of services necessary to maintain mental and physical health. It includes physical, verbal, emotional and sexual abuse.
Failure to provide the care, services or supervision a client needs to maintain physical or mental health, whether by the agency, a caregiver or a client's own caretaker or by self-neglect.
The improper or illegal use of a client's funds, property or assets for another person's profit or advantage, including theft, coercion and misuse of client credit or bank cards.
The program of the county DSS that receives and evaluates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of disabled and older adults.

procedures: At hire and annually, the Administrator trains each employee on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, and on this policy (PER-06, PER-05). Attendance is documented.

At admission, the Service Supervisor gives the client and family the written client rights notice (CLN-01), explains the right to be free from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and gives the agency's complaint procedure and phone number (CLN-02).
Any employee who sees, suspects or is told of possible abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client calls 911 first if the client is in immediate danger (ADM-02).

The employee immediately notifies the Administrator, or the Service Supervisor/RN if the Administrator cannot be reached, by phone at [PHONE]. The employee does not investigate or confront the person suspected, and does not delay a report to find proof.

The employee, or the Administrator for the agency, reports the suspicion to the county DSS Adult Protective Services immediately and no later than the end of the same shift. The report includes the client's name and address, the nature of the concern, the suspected person (if known) and the reporter's name.

The Administrator removes the accused caregiver from the client at once and keeps the caregiver off all assignments with that client pending investigation. The Administrator also considers whether the caregiver should be suspended from all client contact until the investigation is complete.

The Administrator ensures the client is safe and that the client's needs are met by another caregiver. The Service Supervisor/RN arranges for any medical care required and notifies the health care practitioner and, with the client's permission, the family or representative.
For a Medicaid or CAP/DA client, the Administrator also notifies the client's case manager or care advisor of the allegation and of any safety plan within 1 business day.
The Administrator completes an incident report (CLN-15) the same day. It records who, what, when, where, what the employee observed, who was notified and when, and what protective actions were taken.
The Administrator reports to the HCPR as described in CLN-11 when the allegation involves a staff member within the scope of HCPR reporting, and documents the date and method of the report.

The Administrator begins an internal investigation within 72 hours of any client or family complaint, or sooner for allegations of abuse and neglect, and documents the complaint and its resolution (CLN-02). The agency preserves evidence, including schedules, timesheets and EVV records, and interviews the client, the caregiver and any witnesses.

The Administrator cooperates with DSS, law enforcement and DHSR, who start abuse investigations within 24 hours and neglect investigations within 48 hours. The Administrator gives investigators immediate access to records and staff (SUP-02).
The Administrator does not hire or place anyone with a substantiated HCPR finding and verifies the HCPR before hire and as required (PER-07).

When the investigation is complete, the Administrator documents the findings and corrective action. Staff who are found to have abused, neglected or exploited a client are terminated, and the matter is reported as required.
The Administrator informs the client or the client's representative of the outcome of the agency's investigation, within the limits of confidentiality, and documents the notification.
The Administrator prohibits retaliation against any employee or client who reports in good faith, and discipline is applied to anyone who retaliates.
The Administrator reviews all allegations at least annually in the program evaluation to identify trends and training needs (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Receives reports, removes the accused caregiver, ensures reports to DSS and HCPR, investigates, cooperates with agencies and documents the outcome.
Ensures client safety and medical care, notifies the practitioner and family, and arranges replacement caregivers.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, call 911 in an emergency, and never retaliate.
Ensures the agency has resources and policies to protect clients and supports prompt removal of accused staff.

documentation: Abuse, neglect and exploitation training records
Incident report
Copy of report to DSS Adult Protective Services with date and time
HCPR reporting record (see CLN-11)
Investigation file and outcome
Client or family notification record

policies.title: Incident Reporting and Documentation
policies.applies_to: All employees, Service Supervisor/RN, Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure that every injury, fall, property damage event, complaint and other incident involving a client or caregiver is reported, reviewed promptly, documented, analyzed for trends and available for DHSR review.
policies.policy: All injuries, falls, property damage and complaints must be documented on an incident report form. Each incident is reviewed by the Service Supervisor within the same business day it is reported. Results are trended and reviewed in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08). Incident reports are kept available for DHSR review. DHSR may inspect at any time and requires immediate access to premises and records, and failure to allow it terminates the survey (10A NCAC 13J .0904). A client or family complaint is investigated within 72 hours and the complaint and its resolution are documented (G.S. 131E-144.6).

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event involving a client, caregiver or the client's property that causes or could cause harm, loss or a complaint. It includes injuries, falls, medication concerns, property damage or loss, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, equipment failures, exposures to blood or body fluids, threats and complaints.
The agency's standard form on which each incident is described, reviewed and closed.
A pattern across incidents by type, client, caregiver, time or location that points to a possible system problem.

procedures: The caregiver gives first aid or calls 911 as needed to protect the client's safety (ADM-02). Immediate safety comes before paperwork.

The caregiver tells the Service Supervisor by phone immediately, and in all cases before leaving the client's home, about any injury, fall, property damage, medication concern, complaint or other incident. After hours, the caregiver calls the on-call number [PHONE].

The caregiver completes the incident report form within 24 hours of the incident. The form records the client's name, date and time, location, persons involved, a factual description in the caregiver's own words, immediate actions, and who was notified.
If the incident is a late discovery, the caregiver writes the report as soon as it is discovered and marks 'late entry' where appropriate (CLN-12).
The Service Supervisor reviews each incident report within the same business day it is reported. The supervisor signs and dates the review and records any follow-up needed.
The Service Supervisor notifies the client's health care practitioner, the client's family or representative, and a Medicaid case manager or care advisor when appropriate, and documents each call.

If the incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Service Supervisor notifies the Administrator immediately and follows CLN-14. If it involves an exposure to blood or body fluids, the supervisor follows ADM-14.
If the incident is a client or family complaint, the Administrator starts the investigation within 72 hours and documents the complaint and its resolution (CLN-02).
The Service Supervisor determines whether the plan of care needs to change as a result of the incident, and if so makes the change under CLN-06 or CLN-20.

The Administrator reviews the incident reports at least weekly, and reviews all serious incidents the same business day. The Administrator documents the corrective action taken, including retraining or supervision of the caregiver.

The Administrator files the closed incident report in an incident file kept separately from the client record. A note that an incident occurred, and the client's condition after it, is documented in the client's service record, without inserting the incident report itself into the client record.
The Administrator keeps an incident log listing the date, client, incident type, caregiver, follow-up and date closed.
The Administrator reviews the log each quarter for trends and uses the results in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08). Trends are reported to the governing body.
The Administrator keeps incident reports on file for at least 5 years and makes them available to DHSR at any inspection (SUP-02). Reports are produced immediately on request.
The Administrator will not discipline an employee for reporting an incident in good faith.

responsibilities.duty: Respond to the incident, notify the supervisor immediately and complete the incident report within 24 hours.
Reviews every incident the same business day, notifies the practitioner and family, and updates the plan of care.
Ensures follow-up and corrective action, maintains the incident log, trends results for the annual evaluation and produces reports for DHSR.

documentation: Incident report forms with supervisor review signature and date
Incident log
Complaint investigation record
Notification records (practitioner, family, case manager)
Quarterly and annual trend summaries

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and money, prevent financial exploitation, and set clear rules for gifts, shopping and cash handling.
policies.policy: Clients have the right to be free from exploitation and to have their property treated with respect (G.S. 131E-144.3). Staff may not accept gifts, loans or bequests from clients or their families, and may not use client funds or property for personal benefit. Any shopping or cash handling for a client requires a receipt log. Misappropriation of client property is reported to the Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR) and to the county DSS as described in CLN-11 and CLN-14. Because a substantiated HCPR finding bars employment (10A NCAC 13J .1003(c)), staff understand that a substantiated misappropriation finding ends their ability to work in home care in North Carolina.

definitions.definition: Money, goods, services, favors or anything of value given to a staff member by a client or a client's family, other than ordinary thanks.
The unauthorized taking, use or misuse of a client's money, property or belongings.
A written record of money received from or spent for a client, with receipts attached, signed by the caregiver and the client or representative.

procedures: At orientation and every year, the Administrator trains staff on this policy and each employee signs an acknowledgment (PER-06, PER-05).

At admission, the Service Supervisor explains to the client and family that staff may not accept gifts, loans or bequests, and may not borrow money or items, sell anything to the client, or be named in the client's will or as beneficiary or power of attorney.

Caregivers politely decline all gifts of money or valuables. If a gift cannot be declined without distress to the client, the caregiver accepts it only to hand over to the supervisor and reports it the same day. The Administrator returns it with an explanation or records its disposition.
Caregivers never use a client's money, credit or debit card, checks, bank account, PIN, passwords or prescriptions for personal benefit. They do not ask a client to sign any document for them.
Caregivers do not use a client's belongings, vehicle, phone or food for personal use.
Shopping or errands involving client money are done only if they are on the plan of care. The caregiver and client agree on the amount in advance.

For each purchase, the caregiver completes the receipt log with the date, amount given, the items bought, the amount spent and the change returned, and obtains the original store receipt. The client or representative signs the log at the time the change is returned.
Caregivers count cash with the client at the beginning and end of the errand when possible and never keep client cash overnight.

The caregiver notes valuable items in the home on the assessment only as the client lists them. The caregiver reports any lost, missing or damaged item to the supervisor immediately and completes an incident report within 24 hours (CLN-15).
The Service Supervisor reviews receipt logs at each monthly record review and at supervisory visits and compares them with the plan of care.
The Administrator starts an inquiry of any reported missing item or irregularity within 72 hours and documents the outcome (CLN-02).

If misappropriation or exploitation is suspected, the employee notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator removes the caregiver from the client, reports to the county DSS, and reports to the HCPR as described in CLN-14 and CLN-11. The agency does not wait for proof before reporting.
The Administrator encourages the client to report the matter to law enforcement and, with the client's permission, assists in the report.
The Administrator verifies HCPR status before hire (PER-07) so that no one with a substantiated finding is placed in a client's home.
An employee who violates this policy is subject to discipline up to and including termination (PER-09).

responsibilities.duty: Decline gifts, never use client money or property for personal benefit, and keep a receipt log for any shopping or cash handling.
Explains the policy to clients, reviews receipt logs and follows up on reports of missing items.
Investigates reports, removes accused caregivers and reports misappropriation to DSS and the HCPR.

documentation: Staff acknowledgment of the gifts and property policy
Client receipt logs with store receipts
Incident reports for missing or damaged property
Investigation records and reports to DSS and the HCPR
Gift disposition record

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and applicants for service
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To make sure that every person who seeks or receives services from [AGENCY NAME] is treated equally and with dignity, can understand the services and their rights, and receives reasonable accommodations for disability.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in acceptance of clients or in the services provided on any protected basis, including race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, age, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity, or source of payment. This policy supports the client's right to dignity and respect (G.S. 131E-144.3) and the agency's duty to comply with all federal, state and local law (10A NCAC 13J .0906), including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

[AGENCY NAME] provides interpreters and translated documents at no cost to clients who have limited English proficiency or who are deaf or hard of hearing. The agency accommodates disabilities, including communication needs. The only basis for declining or discharging a client is the one set out in CLN-04 and CLN-10, such as the agency's inability to safely meet the client's needs within the agency's scope of services and service area, and never a protected characteristic.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to take part in services without language help.
A person who is fluent in English and in the client's language, is trained in interpreting, and keeps client information confidential.

A modification or adjustment that enables a person with a disability to receive services equally, for example large-print documents, a sign language interpreter or a change in how information is delivered.

procedures: At the first contact, the Intake Coordinator asks every applicant and caller what language they prefer to speak and read and whether they need help communicating or any accommodation for a disability. The answers are recorded in the client record.

If the person needs language help, the Intake Coordinator arranges a qualified interpreter, by phone or in person, from [INTERPRETER SERVICE/VENDOR], at no cost to the client. The agency does not charge for interpretation or translation.

Staff do not require or ask clients to bring their own interpreter. A family member or friend interprets only if the client asks for it after being told that a free interpreter is available, and the request is documented. Staff do not use minor children to interpret except in an emergency.

The Service Supervisor provides the client rights notice (CLN-01), the service agreement (CLN-18), the complaint procedure (CLN-02) and the plan of care (CLN-06) in the client's language or, if no written translation exists, reviews them orally through an interpreter and documents it.

For a client who is deaf or hard of hearing or blind or has low vision, the Service Supervisor arranges effective communication, such as a sign language interpreter, written communication, large print or reading documents aloud, at no cost.

The Intake Coordinator accepts or declines each referral using only the criteria in CLN-04: whether the client's needs can be met safely within the agency's scope of service and geographic service area and whether a qualified caregiver is available. The decision is documented on the referral record.

Staff do not refuse a referral, reduce services, or change caregivers because of a client's protected characteristic, source of payment or disability. They do not harass or demean clients for any such reason.

The Service Supervisor considers each client's request for reasonable accommodation and documents the request, the decision and any change to the plan of care. A request is denied only when it would fundamentally change the services or pose a safety risk, and the Administrator approves any denial and records the reason.

Where the client's language or culture affects care, the Service Supervisor assigns, where possible, a caregiver who speaks the client's language, and respects the client's preferences and practices in the plan of care.
