Caregivers who are bilingual may interpret only if they are qualified and the Service Supervisor has approved it. Bilingual caregivers are not asked to interpret for tasks outside their duties.
The Administrator posts or provides to clients a notice that language assistance and accommodation are free and tells them whom to call to ask for it [PHONE].
The Administrator trains all staff at orientation and annually on this policy and on how to access interpreters (PER-06, PER-05).

A client or employee who believes he or she has been discriminated against may file a complaint under CLN-02, without retaliation. The Administrator investigates within 72 hours and documents the resolution. The client may also contact DHSR at 919-855-4620 or a federal civil rights agency.
The Administrator reviews language and accommodation requests, and any discrimination complaints, in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nondiscrimination, contracts with interpreter services, approves any denial of accommodation and investigates complaints.
Asks about language and accommodation needs at first contact, arranges interpreters and applies the acceptance criteria uniformly.
Provides documents in a language and format the client can use and documents accommodations in the plan of care.
Treat every client with dignity, do not discriminate, and use qualified interpreters.

documentation: Language preference and accommodation needs in the client record
Interpreter use log
Translated or oral-review documentation for rights notice, service agreement and plan of care
Accommodation request and decision record
Discrimination complaint investigation records
Staff training records

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Service Supervisor, RN, intake and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or representative receives a written service agreement and a written statement of charges before services begin, and understands rates, minimum hours, cancellation terms, payment methods and key agency rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every client, before services start, a signed written service agreement and a written statement of charges. Under G.S. 131E-144.3, clients have the right to a written statement of charges. Under G.S. 131E-144.4, we give each client the declaration of home care clients' rights, the client-responsibility policies, the agency complaint contact, and the address and phone number of the DHSR Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section, at the initial evaluation visit or before services begin. We keep a signed receipt in the client record. The agreement discloses rates, minimum hours, cancellation terms and payment methods. It also states the agency no-smoking rule (CLN-07) and the DHSR notice at signing. The private-pay agreement template is reviewed by the agency's attorney before use and again whenever it is materially changed. Services are never started on an unsigned agreement unless the client's condition requires emergency action under ADM-02. Medicaid State Plan PCS and CAP/DA clients are billed to Medicaid according to the authorization (MED-01, MED-02). The agency does not bill those clients for authorized, covered services.

definitions.definition: The written contract between the agency and the client or legal representative that describes services, charges, responsibilities and terms.
A written list of what the client will be charged, including rates, minimum hours, cancellation fees and billing frequency.
Services paid for by the client, family or another third party other than Medicaid.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as a health care agent or guardian.

procedures: Before the agreement is first used, the Administrator has the agency's attorney review the private-pay service agreement template and the statement of charges. The Administrator keeps the attorney review date and the approved template in the administrative file.

The Administrator sets private-pay rates, minimum hours per visit, cancellation terms and payment methods in writing on the Rate Schedule: [PRIVATE-PAY HOURLY RATE], [MINIMUM HOURS PER VISIT], [CANCELLATION NOTICE AND FEE] and [ACCEPTED PAYMENT METHODS]. The Administrator reviews the Rate Schedule at least annually.

At intake (CLN-04), the Service Supervisor or RN explains the payment source: private pay, Medicaid State Plan PCS, or CAP/DA. For Medicaid clients, staff confirm that an authorization exists or is pending (MED-01, MED-02).

At the initial evaluation visit, and in any case before services start, the RN or Service Supervisor gives the client or representative the declaration of home care clients' rights, the client-responsibility policies, the agency complaint contact ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]), and the DHSR Acute and Home Care Licensure and Certification Section address and phone (919-855-4620).
The staff member reviews each document aloud or in the client's preferred language or format (CLN-17), and answers questions.

The staff member gives the client a written statement of charges that lists rate by service type, minimum hours, cancellation terms, any charges for supplies or mileage, billing frequency and payment methods. Medicaid clients receive a statement that covered, authorized services are billed to Medicaid and lists any non-covered services they may choose to pay for privately.

The staff member discloses the no-smoking rule (CLN-07), the 24-hour on-call and supervisor contact number ([PHONE]), the right to refuse services, and the grievance process (CLN-02), and points out the DHSR notice. The client or representative initials each item on the disclosure checklist.

The client or representative and an agency representative sign and date the service agreement. The client signs a separate receipt for the rights declaration, client-responsibility policies, complaint contact and DHSR information.

The agency gives the client a complete copy of the signed agreement, statement of charges and rights documents. A copy goes in the client record, and the home copy stays in the client's home with the plan of care.

If the client or representative declines to sign, the staff member records the date, the reason and who was present. The Service Supervisor notifies the Administrator, and no non-emergency service starts until the issue is resolved.
Billing staff invoice only for services actually delivered, in the units and at the rate stated in the agreement or the Medicaid authorization. Invoices go out on the schedule in the agreement.

The Administrator gives at least [30] days' written notice before any private-pay rate change and obtains the client's written acknowledgment. If the client does not accept the change, the Service Supervisor follows CLN-10 for discontinuation, including required notice.
When the client's authorization, payment source or plan of care changes, the Service Supervisor updates the agreement or issues an addendum, and the client or representative signs it.
Billing staff handle billing disputes and refund requests in writing within [10] business days. Unresolved complaints go to the Administrator under CLN-02.

The Administrator audits a sample of new client records quarterly to confirm signed agreements, statements of charges and rights receipts are present before the first date of service. Findings go into the program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement and Rate Schedule, obtains attorney review, and audits records for compliance.
Explains and delivers the rights and charge documents, collects signatures and files them before services begin.
Invoice according to the agreement or authorization, and answer billing questions.
Reviews and signs the agreement, pays charges as agreed, and tells the agency about any change in payment source.

documentation: Signed service agreement and statement of charges
Signed receipt for the rights declaration, client-responsibility policies, complaint contact and DHSR address and phone
Disclosure checklist initialed by client (rates, minimum hours, cancellation, payment methods, no-smoking rule, DHSR notice)
Rate Schedule and attorney review record
Rate-change notices and acknowledgments
Records of any billing dispute and its resolution

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduler, Service Supervisor, RN, aides and on-call staff
policies.purpose: To make sure scheduled services are delivered as planned, that staff absence is covered, and that clients and supervisors are told promptly of any missed visit and a replacement is arranged.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts clients only when it has enough staff to provide the services in the plan of care, including coverage when staff are absent (10A NCAC 13J .1101). When a scheduled visit cannot be made, the agency notifies the client and the Service Supervisor, arranges a replacement, and logs every missed visit and the reason. Under G.S. 131E-144.3, clients have access to on-call staff and to a supervisor. The agency gives every client a number that is answered during all hours of service, [PHONE], and the Service Supervisor's contact information. Continuity of care is protected by assigning a primary aide and a backup aide who are competent for the client's tasks (PER-02).

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not start within [30] minutes of the scheduled time, or is not made at all, for any reason.
A qualified aide or other worker who is competent in the client's care tasks and who covers the visit.
A designated agency staff member reachable by phone at all hours services are provided.

procedures: At intake (CLN-04), the Scheduler and Service Supervisor confirm current staff capacity, including backup aides, before accepting a client. They record this on the intake checklist.

The Scheduler assigns a primary aide and at least one backup aide for each client. Only aides who have demonstrated the client's tasks are assigned (PER-02, CLN-13). The Scheduler gives each client a written schedule and updates it whenever it changes.
The Scheduler maintains a list of available substitute aides and the RN on-call roster, and posts the on-call number at the office.
An aide who cannot work a scheduled visit calls the Scheduler or on-call number as early as possible, and at least [2] hours before the visit when possible. Texting alone is not acceptable notice.
The Scheduler tells the client or representative by phone as soon as an absence is known and records the time of the call.

The Scheduler offers a replacement aide. If a qualified replacement is found, the Scheduler gives the client the replacement's name and arrival time and briefs the replacement on the plan of care before the visit.

If no replacement can be found, the Scheduler immediately notifies the Service Supervisor. The Service Supervisor calls the client, offers the earliest alternative time, and contacts the family or representative per the client's wishes.

For a client whose missed visit creates a health or safety risk (for example, needs help with eating, toileting or medication reminders), the Service Supervisor or RN decides the same day on additional steps. These include backup staff, a welfare check by a family member or contact, or referral to another provider under CLN-03 and CLN-09. If the client is in danger, staff call 911 (ADM-02).

If an aide arrives and the client is not at home or does not answer, the aide follows the no-answer protocol: wait [15] minutes, call the client and the emergency contact, call the Service Supervisor, and do not leave until the Service Supervisor directs. If the Service Supervisor suspects the client is in danger, the aide or Service Supervisor calls 911 for a welfare check.

The Scheduler records every missed visit on the Missed Visit Log: date, client, aide, reason (staff illness, no-show, client cancellation, transportation, other), who was notified and when, the replacement or rescheduled visit, and any client impact.
For Medicaid clients, the Scheduler makes sure the electronic visit record and any manual correction match what actually happened (MED-03).

A client may reach the on-call staff and a supervisor at any time services are provided. The aide reminds the client of these numbers at the first visit, and they are printed on the client's copy of the plan of care and agreement.
If an aide has repeated absences or is late, the Service Supervisor counsels the aide and records the counseling in the personnel record (PER-09).
The Service Supervisor reviews the Missed Visit Log monthly. The Administrator reviews trends quarterly and reports them in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).
If missed visits show the agency cannot meet a client's needs, the Service Supervisor follows CLN-10, including required notice, before reducing or ending services.

responsibilities.duty: Builds schedules with backup coverage, arranges replacements, notifies clients, and keeps the Missed Visit Log.
Decides on safety follow-up, reviews the log monthly, and counsels staff.
Gives as much advance notice as possible and follows the no-answer protocol.
Makes sure there is staff capacity, an on-call roster, and a review of trends.

documentation: Missed Visit Log
Client schedules and backup assignments
On-call roster
Notes of client, family and supervisor notifications
Staff counseling records
Quarterly trend review within the program evaluation

policies.title: Change in Client Condition
policies.applies_to: Aides, RN, Service Supervisor
policies.purpose: To make sure any change in a client's physical, mental or home condition is reported at once to the RN, assessed, reflected in the plan of care, and communicated to the physician or other prescriber, and to the family or representative.
policies.policy: Aides report any change in a client's condition to the RN immediately (10A NCAC 13J .1107). The RN reassesses and updates the plan of care (10A NCAC 13J .1202). When physician orders are required, the agency notifies the physician of the change (10A NCAC 13J .1202). Any new or changed order is signed by the prescriber, and the original goes into the client record. Care may continue on a verbal order in the interim (10A NCAC 13J .1302(a)). The family or representative is notified according to the client's wishes. In an emergency, staff call 911 first and follow ADM-02.

definitions.definition: A new or worsening symptom, injury, fall, behavior or cognitive change, change in ability to perform ADLs, change in medication use or tolerance, or change in the home that affects safety or care needs.
The written plan developed with the client, signed by the practitioner and client, stating service type, frequency and duration, level of assistance per ADL, restrictions, safety measures and goals.
The physician or other practitioner who signs orders when orders are required.

procedures: The aide identifies a change in condition during a visit, or learns of one from the client or family. Examples are a fall, new confusion, a new skin problem, a change in eating or toileting, or a refusal of care or medications.
If the situation is life-threatening, the aide calls 911 first, stays with the client, then calls the RN or on-call supervisor. Follow ADM-02 and CLN-15.
For any other change, the aide calls the RN or on-call supervisor immediately, before leaving the home if possible. The aide does not wait until the next scheduled contact or timesheet submission.

The aide describes what was observed, when it started, what the client reported and what the aide did. The aide does not diagnose, give medical advice, change medication use, or change the plan of care without RN direction.

The RN decides whether the client needs emergency care, a physician call or an agency reassessment, and tells the aide what to do. The RN documents the report and instructions in the client record the same day.

The aide writes a factual note on the visit record the same day, including time of report and the RN's instructions. The aide follows incident procedures in CLN-15 when an injury, fall or unusual event occurred.

The RN contacts the client and reviews the situation by phone the same day. The RN reassesses the client in the home when clinical judgment indicates, and in any case within [24 hours] for a significant change.

The RN updates the plan of care to reflect the new needs: type, frequency and duration of service, level of assistance per ADL, restrictions, safety measures and goals (10A NCAC 13J .1202). The RN signs and dates the update.

When physician orders are required for in-home aide services, the RN notifies the physician of the change and requests any new orders. Verbal orders are documented immediately, read back and later signed by the prescriber. The agency obtains the signed original and files it in the client record (10A NCAC 13J .1302(a)).

The RN gives the revised plan of care to the client or representative for review and signature, as in CLN-06. The updated copy is placed in the home and the superseded version is marked as such in the record.

The RN or Service Supervisor notifies the family or representative of the change according to the client's wishes recorded at intake. The agency records the date, time, person contacted and what was said. If the client does not want a family member notified, the agency respects that unless the client lacks capacity or there is an emergency.

The Service Supervisor informs the Scheduler of any changes in service hours or staffing. For Medicaid clients, the Service Supervisor determines whether the change requires a new or revised authorization, service plan or CAP/DA case manager notification (MED-01, MED-02).

The RN informs the aides assigned to the client of the revised plan of care and confirms in writing that each aide understands it. Any new task is demonstrated by the RN to the aide and documented (PER-02).
If the change shows the agency can no longer safely meet the client's needs, the RN and Service Supervisor follow CLN-10 and CLN-03, including required notice and referral to other agencies.
The Service Supervisor reviews the change in condition in the next 90-day client record review (ADM-09, CLN-06) and notes patterns in the program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Reports any change in condition to the RN immediately, calls 911 in an emergency, and documents factually.
Directs the immediate response, reassesses the client, updates the plan of care, and notifies the physician when orders are required.
Coordinates scheduling, family or representative notification, and authorization changes.
Reviews trends and makes sure staff are trained on reporting.

documentation: Aide visit note recording the change and time of report to the RN
RN notes of the report, instructions, reassessment and follow-up
Updated plan of care with signatures
Physician or prescriber notification and orders, including the signed original
Record of family or representative notification
Incident report when applicable (CLN-15)

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: Aides, Service Supervisor, RN, Administrator
policies.purpose: To set safe conditions under which caregivers may transport clients, and to make sure that transport occurs only when the plan of care authorizes it and the caregiver is competent to perform it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] aides transport a client only when the client's plan of care specifically authorizes transport. Under 10A NCAC 13J .1110, caregivers are assigned only tasks they have demonstrated to the health care practitioner, so transport, including any assistance getting in and out of the vehicle, is assigned only to an aide whose competence is documented. Every driver must hold a valid driver's license, valid vehicle registration and current auto insurance, and everyone in the vehicle must wear a seat belt. For Medicaid clients, transport is also provided only where the authorization or service plan permits it. Staff document trip purpose, mileage and any incident.

definitions.definition: Driving a client in an agency or staff-member vehicle, or in the client's own vehicle, for errands, appointments or activities authorized in the plan of care.
A trip with a purpose and frequency stated in the signed plan of care.
The record of date, purpose, destination, mileage and any incident for each transport.

procedures: During the initial assessment (CLN-05), the RN decides whether the client needs or wants transport and writes the purpose, destinations and frequency into the plan of care. If the plan of care does not authorize transport, aides do not provide it.
For Medicaid clients, the Service Supervisor checks that the authorization or service plan allows the transport and the time spent. If it is not allowed, the aide does not transport.

The RN assesses the client's ability to get in and out of a vehicle, mobility aids, seating, behavior and any safety risk. The RN states in the plan of care the level of assistance and any restrictions, such as no transport while the client is unsteady or agitated.

The RN demonstrates or verifies the aide's competence in assisting with vehicle transfers and securing mobility aids before assigning the aide transport tasks. The RN records the demonstration (PER-02). Competence for vehicle transfers is not assumed from general aide training.

Before any aide drives clients, the Service Supervisor verifies and copies the aide's valid driver's license, vehicle registration and proof of current auto insurance. The Service Supervisor checks them again annually and whenever a license or policy expires, and files copies in the personnel record (PER-03).
If the agency's liability insurance covers transport, the Administrator confirms the coverage with [INSURER] and keeps proof. Staff are told in writing which vehicles and trips are covered.

Before each trip, the aide confirms with the client the purpose and destination, makes sure the vehicle is safe to drive and works properly, and does not drive when impaired by medication or fatigue. The aide does not use a handheld phone while driving.

Everyone in the vehicle wears a seat belt. The aide does not begin driving until the client is seated and belted. Wheelchairs and walkers are stored so they do not become hazards. The aide does not transport more passengers than seat belts.
The aide does not leave a client alone in the vehicle. The aide does not make unauthorized stops, does not transport other people, and does not conduct personal business during the trip.

The aide records each trip on the Trip Log: date, purpose, destination, start and end odometer readings or miles, and signature of the client or representative where possible. Mileage is recorded only for authorized trips.

If any incident occurs during transport (accident, fall, illness, behavior concern, vehicle breakdown), the aide first ensures safety and calls 911 if needed. The aide then calls the Service Supervisor immediately, and completes an incident report the same day (CLN-15).
After a crash, the aide exchanges information as required by law, cooperates with law enforcement, and does not discuss fault with other parties. The Administrator notifies the insurer.
The Service Supervisor reviews Trip Logs monthly against the plan of care and billing, and corrects any trips outside the plan. Misuse of transport is addressed under PER-09 and ADM-17.
The agency does not require clients to use agency transport and tells clients of other transportation options on request (CLN-03).
The Administrator reviews transport incidents and compliance in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Authorizes transport in the plan of care, assesses client safety, and verifies the aide's vehicle-transfer competence.
Verifies license, registration and insurance, reviews Trip Logs, and responds to incidents.
Transports only authorized trips, follows safety rules, and logs mileage and incidents.
Maintains insurance coverage and reviews transport safety trends.

documentation: Plan of care showing transport authorization and restrictions
Aide competence record for vehicle transfers
Copies of driver's license, registration and insurance, with annual verification dates
Trip Logs
Incident reports for any transport incident
Insurance coverage confirmation

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, RN, Service Supervisor, Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from hazards in client homes and from violence or threats, and to make sure unsafe situations are assessed at intake, caregivers may leave unsafe situations, and incidents are reported and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free from recognized hazards under the OSHA General Duty Clause. Our infection control and safety practices follow 10A NCAC 13J .1003(a) and 29 CFR 1910, which 13J incorporates by reference. A home safety assessment is completed at intake, as part of the home suitability review under our intake policy (CLN-04). Staff may leave an unsafe situation at any time without penalty and must report it to the supervisor. Workplace violence incidents are reported to the supervisor immediately and documented. The agency does not retaliate against any staff member for reporting a hazard or leaving an unsafe situation in good faith.

definitions.definition: A review of the client's home and surroundings at intake for hazards to the client and to staff, such as unsafe structures, pests, weapons, aggressive animals, hostile persons, smoking or oxygen use, and infection risks.
Any physical assault, threat, harassment, intimidation or other aggressive behavior directed at staff by a client, family member, visitor or coworker, including sexual harassment.
Any condition in which a caregiver reasonably believes there is an imminent risk to personal safety or health.

procedures: During the initial in-home assessment (CLN-05), the RN completes the Home Safety Assessment checklist. It covers entrances and lighting, structural and fire hazards, smoke detectors, pests, weapons, aggressive pets, substance use, hostile persons, infection hazards, and the neighborhood. The RN records hazards and the plan to reduce them.

The RN reviews the results with the client or representative and asks them to correct hazards that can be corrected, such as securing pets, locking up weapons and clearing pathways. The RN documents the discussion and the client's response.

If the home is not suitable and the hazards cannot be reduced, the Service Supervisor and Administrator decide whether the agency can accept or continue the client, and follow CLN-04 and CLN-10, including referral to other agencies.
The RN shares relevant safety information with each assigned aide before the first visit, and the plan of care includes safety measures for the home.

Aides follow safe work practices: lock the car, tell the office the visit schedule, carry a charged phone, park in a well-lit spot when possible, and do not enter the home when the situation looks unsafe.

Hands-on staff follow the agency's infection control practices, use personal protective equipment, and receive annual airborne and bloodborne pathogen training under the exposure control plan (ADM-10, ADM-11, ADM-14, PER-05).

Any staff member who feels threatened or unsafe may leave the home immediately. If a client is in immediate danger and the aide cannot remain, the aide calls 911 and the supervisor before leaving, and does not abandon a client who cannot be left safely without notifying the supervisor.

The staff member calls the Service Supervisor or on-call supervisor immediately after leaving or when any threat, assault, harassment or unsafe condition occurs. The supervisor decides on next steps, which may include sending another worker or suspending visits until the hazard is resolved.
If someone is injured or in danger, staff call 911 first. After a physical assault, the agency helps the employee get medical care and reports the incident to law enforcement when appropriate.

The staff member completes an incident report the same day (CLN-15), describing who, what, when, where, witnesses and actions taken. The Service Supervisor reviews it and gives it to the Administrator within [24 hours].

The Administrator investigates the report, interviews those involved, decides on corrective action, and records the outcome. Corrective action may include a revised plan of care, assigning two staff, a client or family behavior agreement, a change in staff assignment, or discharge under CLN-10.

The Administrator offers affected staff a debrief, time off if needed, and information on workers' compensation and employee assistance resources. Reporting a hazard or incident is never grounds for discipline.
If workplace violence involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of the client, or a client-caused injury suggests a client needs help, staff follow CLN-14 as well.

The Administrator keeps a log of workplace violence and safety incidents and reviews it at least quarterly. The review includes trends by client, location and cause, and is reported in the annual program evaluation (ADM-08).
The Service Supervisor reviews this policy with all staff at orientation (PER-06) and annually in in-service education (PER-05), and documents the training.

responsibilities.duty: Completes the home safety assessment at intake, records hazards and safety measures, and informs assigned aides.
Responds to reports, adjusts assignments, and follows up with staff.
Follows safe work practices, may leave an unsafe situation, and reports hazards and incidents immediately.
Investigates incidents, takes corrective action, prevents retaliation, and reviews trends.

documentation: Home Safety Assessment checklist in the client record
Incident reports for violence, threats and unsafe situations
Investigation notes and corrective action
Workplace violence and safety incident log
Training records for safety, infection control and bloodborne/airborne pathogens
Quarterly review and annual program evaluation notes

policies.title: Personnel Qualifications, Nurse Aide Registry and Credential Verification
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Service Supervisor, RN, Scheduler, aides, and anyone who hires or assigns staff
policies.purpose: To set the qualifications for each position, to make sure aides who give extensive assistance are on the Nurse Aide Registry, and to verify licenses, registrations and core skills at hire and annually.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 13J .1001(a)(7) — personnel qualifications. The governing body adopts the following qualifications. (1) Agency Director: one of the following. The person is a licensed health care practitioner; or has two years of supervisory or management experience in home care or another provider licensed under G.S. 131E or 122C; or holds a bachelor's degree in health, business or public administration science plus one year of supervisory or management experience in home care or another licensed health care program. If the agency is licensed only for companion, sitter and respite services, the lighter standard in ADM-05 applies. (2) RN / Service Supervisor: a registered nurse with a current North Carolina license in good standing, available for supervision and consultation during all hours aide services are provided, who makes the home visit to develop the plan of care; the agency additionally requires [ONE] year of clinical experience. (3) Scheduler: at least a high school diploma or GED, with the training in the agency's scheduling, missed-visit and confidentiality procedures. (4) In-home aide: age 18 or older, able to read, write and follow written instructions, with competence in the tasks assigned. Aides who give extensive assistance must be on the Nurse Aide Registry (10A NCAC 13J .1107). For aides hired after 4/1/2009 who are not on the registry, an RN verifies six core skills before the aide works alone: mobility/transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating and continence care (10A NCAC 13J .1003(g)). Staff must hold current North Carolina licenses and registrations as required (10A NCAC 13J .0906). The agency verifies licenses and registrations at hire and annually. No one is assigned a task for which the person lacks the required qualification.

definitions.definition: The North Carolina registry of nurse aides maintained by DHSR. Listing shows completion of an approved nurse aide training and competency evaluation, and the person's status for abuse findings.
The level of help for an activity of daily living (ADL) in which the aide provides more than limited help with the activity, as stated in the plan of care for each ADL.
The six skills an RN must verify for aides hired after 4/1/2009 who are not on the registry: mobility/transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating and continence care.
Primary-source confirmation that a license, certification or registry listing is current and in good standing.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written qualification standard and job description for each position (ADM-07) and uses them in every recruitment. The governing body reviews these qualifications with the policies (ADM-16).

Before hiring or appointing an Agency Director, the governing body verifies that the person meets one of the three qualification paths. It collects proof: license verification, résumé with dates and references for supervisory or management experience, or a degree transcript plus experience proof. Document the path used in the personnel record. For companion/sitter/respite-only services, apply ADM-05.

Before assigning an RN or Service Supervisor, the Administrator verifies the North Carolina RN license on the NC Board of Nursing website, prints the result with the date, and checks for discipline. The Administrator confirms the RN is available for supervision and consultation during all hours aide services are provided and can make the home visit for the plan of care.

The Administrator verifies the Scheduler's education and reviews the person's training in the scheduling, missed visit, confidentiality and emergency procedures (CLN-19, ADM-15) before the person begins scheduling.

For each aide applicant, the Service Supervisor or Administrator verifies identity and age, and checks the Nurse Aide Registry on the DHSR website before the first client assignment. The staff member prints the result with the date and files it in the personnel record. The same check confirms that there is no finding against the person on the registry.

The Administrator checks the Health Care Personnel Registry and completes the criminal background investigation before assignment (PER-07). No one is assigned to clients before these checks are complete.

If the aide is on the Nurse Aide Registry in good standing, the aide may be assigned tasks, including extensive assistance, for which the aide has completed orientation and shown competence (PER-02, PER-06).

If the aide is not on the Nurse Aide Registry and was hired after 4/1/2009, the aide may not be assigned extensive assistance. Before the aide works alone with any client, an RN directly observes the aide and verifies the six core skills: mobility/transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating and continence care. The RN signs and dates the competency record for each skill.

If an aide who is not on the Nurse Aide Registry does not pass a core skill, the RN gives instruction and re-evaluates. The aide is not assigned any task related to the failed skill until the RN verifies it.

The Service Supervisor reviews each client's plan of care before assigning an aide, and assigns an aide for extensive assistance only if the aide is on the Nurse Aide Registry (10A NCAC 13J .1107). The Scheduler checks the aide qualification flag in the schedule before each assignment.
The Service Supervisor confirms that aides are assigned only tasks demonstrated to the health care practitioner and documented (PER-02, CLN-13).

Staff who hold a professional license or other credential (RN, LPN, CNA, etc.) must hold it current. They must tell the Administrator within [2] business days of any suspension, expiration, discipline or lapse.

The Administrator verifies every license, registration and listing again at least annually, and before the expiration date for any license. The Administrator prints the primary-source verification, records the date and initials it. Verification is done again at each change in role.

If a license or registration lapses or a negative finding is found, the Administrator removes the person from assignments that require the credential at once, tells the Service Supervisor and Scheduler, and acts under HR procedures. The Administrator reports required findings under CLN-11.
The Administrator keeps all qualification proof and verification records in the personnel record (PER-03), and keeps them available for the DHSR surveyor (PRR-01).
The Administrator reviews the qualification table for all staff at least annually and reports results to the governing body. The governing body updates this policy as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts these qualification standards and verifies the Agency Director's qualification.
Verifies credentials at hire and annually, runs registry checks, and removes staff from assignments when credentials lapse.
Verifies the six core skills of aides not on the registry and assigns only qualified aides to extensive assistance.
Assigns staff according to the qualification flags and plan of care.
Keep licenses and registrations current and report changes within 2 business days.

documentation: Qualification evidence for each position (license verification, degree, experience proof, résumé)
Nurse Aide Registry check with date, at hire and annually
RN verification of the six core skills for aides hired after 4/1/2009 who are not on the registry
Annual license and registration verification record
Qualification table showing each staff member's position, registry status and assignable tasks
Governing body review minutes

policies.title: Competency Verification and Skills Validation
policies.applies_to: All in-home aides and caregivers (employees and contract staff), the Registered Nurse (RN), the Service Supervisor and the Agency Director
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver of [AGENCY NAME] is assigned only to tasks that the caregiver has been trained for and has shown he or she can perform safely. Competency is demonstrated to a health care practitioner and documented on a skills checklist signed by the RN.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns a caregiver only to tasks the caregiver has demonstrated to the RN or other health care practitioner, and the agency keeps documentation of each demonstration. A caregiver is not given a client assignment until competency is verified for every task on that client's plan of care. For an aide hired after April 1, 2009 who is not on the NC Nurse Aide Registry, an RN verifies six core skills before assignment: mobility and transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating, and continence care. The RN records verification on the agency Skills Competency Checklist and signs it. Competency is reassessed periodically and after any change in task. Supervision may be delegated by this policy only to the extent that the RN stays available and accountable. For non-hands-on staff (companion, sitter and respite), the agency follows the contact and home-visit schedule in this policy. Staff are assigned only to duties for which they are trained, competent and licensed. This policy meets Personnel Policies: .1003(e)(g); .1110(a)(b)(c); .1504(1) (Competency verification, skills validation/checklist policy).

definitions.definition: Direct observation by the RN or other health care practitioner of a caregiver performing a task correctly, safely and respectfully, with the result recorded in writing.
The six skills an RN must verify for an aide hired after April 1, 2009 who is not on the Nurse Aide Registry: mobility/transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating and continence care.
The RN (or other licensed practitioner acting within his or her license) who observes the caregiver and signs the verification.
Companion, sitter and respite staff who do not provide hands-on personal care. Applies only if the agency offers these services (see ADM-05).
The agency form on which each skill is listed with the date, method of demonstration, result and the signatures of the RN and caregiver.

procedures: Before any offer is finalized, the Service Supervisor checks the NC Nurse Aide Registry (see PER-01) and records whether the applicant is listed. The result is filed in the personnel record.
The Agency Director confirms that no caregiver is scheduled for a client until the Service Supervisor has matched the caregiver's signed checklist to the tasks in that client's plan of care.

For an aide hired after April 1, 2009 who is not on the Nurse Aide Registry, the RN observes a return demonstration of each of the six core skills (mobility/transfers, bath/shower, toileting, dressing, eating, continence care) before the aide's first client assignment.

The RN records each skill on the Skills Competency Checklist with the date, method of demonstration (return demonstration on a client, a model or a staff volunteer), result (competent or needs further training), and the RN's printed name, license number and signature. The aide also signs.
If a skill is not demonstrated satisfactorily, the RN provides retraining and repeats the demonstration. The aide is not assigned to that task until the RN has signed the skill as competent.

For an aide who is on the Nurse Aide Registry, the RN or Service Supervisor still reviews the aide's credentials and verifies by demonstration any task on the plan of care that the aide has not already demonstrated to the agency, before assigning that task.

When a plan of care includes a task beyond the six core skills (for example, a task allowed under CLN-13), the RN demonstrates or observes the task and signs a task-specific competency entry for that caregiver before assignment. Tasks outside the caregiver's permitted duties are never assigned.
The Service Supervisor keeps a current competency matrix showing each caregiver's verified tasks and uses it when preparing schedules (see CLN-19).

The RN reassesses each caregiver's competency at least annually, during the annual performance evaluation (see PER-04), by direct observation or return demonstration of the caregiver's most frequently performed tasks.

The RN also reassesses competency, before the caregiver continues the task, whenever: (a) a client's plan of care adds or changes a task; (b) a client's condition changes (see CLN-20); (c) a supervisory visit, complaint or incident shows a performance concern; or (d) the caregiver returns after an absence of six months or more.

Supervision may be delegated to the Service Supervisor by written agency designation (see ADM-06) only when the RN remains available to the Service Supervisor and caregivers and remains accountable for the outcome. The RN reviews supervisory visit reports at least [every 30 days] and signs them.

If the agency provides companion, sitter or respite services, the Service Supervisor verifies that each non-hands-on staff member can perform the assigned tasks safely and that no hands-on care is assigned. The Service Supervisor contacts the client at least every 3 months and visits the home at least every 6 months. The supervisor also makes a visit annually while the aide is in the home. The supervisor is available on-site when necessary.

The Service Supervisor documents each contact and home visit for non-hands-on staff (date, who was present, observations, client feedback and any action taken) and files it in the client record and the personnel record.

Within 5 business days of any completed verification or reassessment, the Service Supervisor files the signed checklist in the caregiver's personnel record (see PER-03). The documents are kept at the licensed site and available to DHSR.

Each year, as part of the annual program evaluation (see ADM-08), the Agency Director reviews competency findings (failed demonstrations, retraining, incidents tied to skill gaps) and adjusts orientation and in-service topics (see PER-05, PER-06).

responsibilities.duty: Observes and verifies the six core skills and task-specific skills, signs the checklist, performs periodic reassessment, and stays available and accountable for any delegated supervision.
Checks the Nurse Aide Registry, maintains the competency matrix, assigns caregivers only to verified tasks, performs non-hands-on staff contacts and visits, and files documentation.
Ensures this policy is followed, stops any assignment made without verified competency, and reviews competency trends annually.
Performs only the tasks he or she has demonstrated, tells the supervisor when asked to do a task not yet demonstrated, and signs the checklist.

documentation: Skills Competency Checklist signed by the RN and the caregiver
Task-specific competency entries
Nurse Aide Registry check result
Competency matrix
Retraining and re-demonstration records
Written delegation of supervision and RN review signatures
Non-hands-on staff contact and home-visit records (3-month, 6-month and annual)
Annual reassessment record

policies.title: Personnel Records Content and Retention
policies.applies_to: All employees and contract staff, the Agency Director, the Service Supervisor and the person who maintains personnel files
policies.purpose: To define what [AGENCY NAME] keeps in each personnel record, where it is kept, who may see it and how long it is retained, so that the agency can show DHSR that every staff member is qualified, screened, trained and evaluated.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel record for each employee. Each record contains: the application; the signed job description; references; TB records; Hepatitis B vaccine record or signed declination; annual bloodborne and airborne pathogen training; the annual evaluation; credential checks; and competency verification. Records are kept for 1 year after termination and are available at the licensed site for DHSR review. This policy meets Personnel Policies: .1003(f) (Personnel records policy and content). This policy, together with PER-05 (In-Service Education) and PER-06 (Orientation), is the written policy on personnel record content, orientation and in-service education required by 10A NCAC 13J .1003(d) (item 1003(d)).

definitions.definition: The file, paper or electronic, kept at the licensed site for each employee, containing the items listed in this policy.
Verification of licenses, certifications, Nurse Aide Registry status, Health Care Personnel Registry status and criminal history results as applicable to the position.
The signed skills checklist and related records described in PER-02.

procedures: The Agency Director designates [PERSONNEL RECORDS CUSTODIAN] to open a personnel record for each person when a conditional offer is made, and the record stays at the licensed site at [ADDRESS].

The custodian places the following in each record: (1) the signed application; (2) the signed job description (see ADM-07); (3) references; (4) TB screening records (see ADM-12); (5) Hepatitis B vaccine record or signed declination (see ADM-13); (6) annual bloodborne and airborne pathogen training records (see ADM-11); (7) the annual evaluation (see PER-04); (8) credential checks; and (9) competency verification (see PER-02).

Credential checks filed in the record include, as applicable: professional license verification, Nurse Aide Registry check (see PER-01), Health Care Personnel Registry check and criminal history result (see PER-07).
The custodian also files orientation records (see PER-06) and in-service attendance records (see PER-05) in each personnel record.

The custodian completes the Personnel Record Review Checklist (see PRR-01) for each new record within 10 business days of the first day of work and gives the Agency Director a list of any missing items.

The Agency Director sets a date within 5 business days to correct each missing item. A caregiver with a missing credential, TB, competency or screening item is not scheduled for client care until it is completed.
Form I-9 employment eligibility documents are completed as 8 USC 1324a requires. They are kept in a separate I-9 file, not in the general personnel record, and kept for the federal retention period.

Confidential items (medical, immunization, TB, background and I-9 information) are kept in a locked cabinet or a password-protected system with access limited to the Agency Director, the custodian and others with a work need (see ADM-15).
The custodian reviews each record every 6 months for expiring items (licenses, TB follow-up, annual training, annual evaluation) and gives the Agency Director a list of items due in the next 60 days.
If records are electronic, the Agency Director makes sure they can be printed or shown to the surveyor at the licensed site on request during an inspection (see SUP-02).

When a person leaves, the custodian records the termination date and the reason on the record and moves it to closed files. The record is retained for 1 year after the termination date, or longer if required by another law, a Medicaid requirement (see ADM-17) or a pending legal matter.
After the retention period, the custodian destroys the record by shredding or secure deletion with the Agency Director's approval and logs the destruction date.
Employees may review their own record on request, in the presence of the custodian, and may add a written statement.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, assigns the custodian, reviews record audits and approves destruction.
Opens and audits records, files documents, controls access and tracks expiration dates and retention.
Gives the custodian competency, evaluation and training documents promptly and does not schedule staff whose records are incomplete.
Provides complete and truthful documents and tells the agency of changes to licenses or certifications.

documentation: Personnel record for each employee (contents listed above)
Personnel Record Review Checklist
Expiration tracking log
Separate I-9 file
Record destruction log
Access log for confidential records

policies.title: Annual Performance Evaluation
policies.applies_to: All employees, including caregivers, the Service Supervisor, the RN and office staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every employee of [AGENCY NAME] receives a documented performance evaluation each year, so that strengths are recognized, problems are corrected and the evaluation is available in the personnel record for DHSR.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes an evaluation for each employee annually and files it in the personnel record. The evaluation is reviewed with the employee, and the employee signs it. This policy meets Personnel Policies: .1003(f)(7) (Annual performance evaluation policy).

definitions.definition: A written assessment of job performance against the employee's signed job description, completed once in each 12-month period.
The anniversary of the employee's hire date. The evaluation must be completed and signed within 30 days before or after that date.
The Service Supervisor for caregivers, and the Agency Director for the Service Supervisor, the RN and office staff.

procedures: The personnel records custodian lists each employee's evaluation due date (hire-date anniversary) and gives the list to the Agency Director and Service Supervisor 45 days before each due date.
The evaluator completes the agency Annual Performance Evaluation form, which rates performance against the tasks and standards in the employee's signed job description (see ADM-07).

For caregivers, the evaluator uses at least: the most recent supervisory visit findings (see CLN-08), attendance and punctuality, documentation accuracy, client and family feedback, complaints and incidents, and adherence to the plan of care, confidentiality, boundaries and no-smoking rules.
For caregivers, the RN or Service Supervisor reassesses competency as required by PER-02 at the time of the evaluation, and the signed checklist is attached to or referenced in the evaluation.

The evaluator confirms that the employee's annual bloodborne and airborne pathogen training and required in-service hours are complete (see PER-05, ADM-11), and records any items not completed with a due date.
The evaluator reconfirms that required licenses or certifications, and Nurse Aide Registry and HCPR status, are current and notes the date of the check (see PER-01, PER-07).
The evaluator meets privately with the employee to review the evaluation, discuss strengths and areas for improvement, and set goals or a written corrective plan with dates.

The employee signs and dates the evaluation to show it was reviewed. If the employee disagrees, he or she may attach a written comment. If the employee refuses to sign, the evaluator writes 'employee declined to sign,' with the date, and a second manager initials it.
The evaluator gives the signed evaluation to the custodian within 5 business days of the review, and the custodian files it in the personnel record (see PER-03). The employee receives a copy.
If the evaluation is overdue, the Agency Director is notified the day after the 30-day window ends, and the evaluation is completed within 10 business days.

Serious concerns found in an evaluation (client safety, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, or misappropriation) are reported immediately under CLN-14 and CLN-11 and are not held for the annual process.

The Agency Director reviews the percentage of evaluations completed on time and the common performance themes each year and uses them in the annual program evaluation (see ADM-08) and in planning in-service topics.

responsibilities.duty: Evaluates the Service Supervisor, RN and office staff, ensures all evaluations are completed on time and acts on reported concerns.
Evaluates caregivers, gathers supervisory visit and client feedback data and holds the review meeting.
Reassesses caregiver competency at the time of the evaluation.
Tracks due dates and files signed evaluations.
Takes part in the review and signs to show it was reviewed.

documentation: Signed Annual Performance Evaluation in each personnel record
Evaluation due-date tracking list
Attached competency reassessment checklist
Written corrective plan, if any
Employee comments or refusal-to-sign note

policies.title: In-Service Education
policies.applies_to: All employees and contract staff, with required hours set by position as stated in this policy
policies.purpose: To provide ongoing training that keeps [AGENCY NAME] staff competent and current on client care, safety and regulatory requirements, and to keep attendance records that show DHSR the training was given.
policies.policy: The state rule does not set a number of in-service hours. [AGENCY NAME] sets its own annual hours in this policy and follows them. Each hands-on caregiver completes at least 12 hours of in-service education in each 12-month period, counted from the date of hire. Non-hands-on staff (companion, sitter and respite staff, if the agency employs them) complete at least 6 hours. Office and supervisory staff complete at least 6 hours relevant to their roles. Hands-on staff also complete annual bloodborne pathogen and airborne pathogen training. The agency keeps in-service attendance records. This policy meets Personnel Policies: .1003(d) in-service (In-service training policy). Together with PER-03 (Personnel Records Content and Retention) and PER-06 (Orientation), it is the written policy on personnel record content, orientation and in-service education required by 10A NCAC 13J .1003(d) (item 1003(d)).

definitions.definition: Training given to staff after orientation, on any approved topic, by the agency or an outside source, with attendance documented.

definitions.term: Annual bloodborne and airborne pathogen training
definitions.definition: Required yearly training for hands-on staff, filed in the personnel record (see ADM-11 and ADM-12).
The 12-month period beginning on the employee's hire date.

procedures: Each December the Agency Director and RN draft an in-service calendar for the next year, based on the annual program evaluation (see ADM-08), incident and complaint trends, competency reassessments (see PER-02), supervisory visit findings and regulatory changes.

The calendar includes at least: infection control and communicable disease (ADM-10); bloodborne pathogens (ADM-11) and airborne pathogens, both annually; client rights (CLN-01); abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting (CLN-14); incident reporting (CLN-15); confidentiality (ADM-15); emergency preparedness (ADM-02); caregiver safety (CLN-22); boundaries (PER-09); and, for staff serving Medicaid clients, EVV and timekeeping (MED-03).

Hands-on caregivers must complete at least 12 hours per training year. Non-hands-on and office staff must complete at least 6 hours. The Agency Director may increase these hours by written revision of this policy (see ADM-16).
The Service Supervisor announces each session at least 14 days ahead and schedules it so that caregivers can attend. Paid time is addressed in PER-08.

The instructor (RN, Agency Director or qualified outside trainer) uses a sign-in sheet showing the topic, date, length in hours, trainer's name and credentials, and each attendee's printed name and signature.
Trainers may use live, video or online sessions. Online or video sessions require a certificate or the employee's signed attestation plus the Service Supervisor's confirmation of the hours.
Where possible, the instructor gives a brief written or oral check on understanding (quiz or return demonstration), and the results are kept with the session record.

Annual bloodborne pathogen and airborne pathogen training is completed by each hands-on employee within 12 months of the previous session. The certificate or sign-in sheet is filed in the personnel record (see PER-03).
The custodian posts each employee's attendance and hours to an in-service log and files the sign-in sheets in the personnel record and in a central in-service binder or folder.
Every quarter the Service Supervisor reviews the log and contacts any employee who is behind on hours. Employees who miss a session make it up within 30 days.

An employee who has not completed the required hours by the end of the training year is not scheduled for new client assignments until a plan to complete them is approved by the Agency Director. The shortfall is noted on the annual evaluation (see PER-04).

If a client's plan of care, a new procedure or a supervisory finding shows that a caregiver needs additional training or competency verification, it is arranged right away and is not held for the next scheduled session (see PER-02).
The Agency Director reviews in-service completion rates each year and reports them in the annual program evaluation (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the annual calendar and required hours, reviews completion and takes corrective action.
Teaches or approves clinical content and verifies understanding.
Schedules sessions, monitors the in-service log and follows up on missed sessions.
Posts attendance and files records.
Attends, signs in and completes the annual hours.

documentation: Annual in-service calendar
Sign-in sheets with topic, date, hours, trainer and signatures
In-service log for each employee
Certificates for online or outside training
Annual bloodborne and airborne pathogen training records
Make-up session records
Annual completion report

policies.title: Orientation
policies.applies_to: All new employees and contract staff before any client assignment
policies.purpose: To make sure every new staff member of [AGENCY NAME] understands client rights, safety, reporting duties and agency procedures before working with any client, and that orientation is documented.
policies.policy: Each new staff member completes orientation before any client assignment. Orientation covers client rights, including training on the Bill of Rights under G.S. 131E-144.5; confidentiality; abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting; infection control; emergencies; the no-smoking rule; and the plan of care. The date and content of orientation are documented in the personnel record. The Agency Director is responsible for implementing the Bill of Rights, and the agency provides the training needed to implement it. Bloodborne pathogen training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 is part of orientation for staff with occupational exposure. This policy meets Personnel Policies: .1003(d) orientation (Orientation policy).

definitions.definition: The structured training that a new employee completes before client assignment, covering the topics listed in this policy.
The NC home care client rights that the agency must implement and train staff on (see CLN-01).
Any scheduled or unscheduled visit to a client's home, including shadow visits in which the new staff member provides care.

procedures: On or before the first day of work, the Service Supervisor gives the new employee the orientation agenda, a copy of the signed job description (ADM-07) and a copy of the agency's policies relevant to the position.

The new employee is not scheduled for any client visit until the Service Supervisor has signed the Orientation Completion Record. Shadowing an experienced caregiver as an observer is allowed before the sign-off if no care is provided and the client has agreed.

The trainer reviews client rights and the Bill of Rights (CLN-01) with the employee, and the employee explains how rights apply in the home (dignity, privacy, consent, complaint process). The Agency Director confirms the training is given, as G.S. 131E-144.5 requires.
The trainer covers confidentiality and HIPAA, the handling of client information and phones or social media (ADM-15), and the employee signs the agency confidentiality agreement.

The trainer covers abuse, neglect and exploitation: how to recognize them, the duty to report immediately to the Service Supervisor or Agency Director, and the Health Care Personnel Registry process (CLN-14, CLN-11).

The trainer covers infection control, standard precautions, hand hygiene, exposure to communicable disease, and bloodborne pathogens as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030, including the exposure control plan and post-exposure steps (ADM-10, ADM-11, ADM-14).
The employee is given TB screening and Hepatitis B vaccine information and a declination form if the vaccine is declined (ADM-12, ADM-13).

The trainer covers emergencies: how to call 911, what to report to the agency, how to respond to falls, fire, severe weather and loss of power, and how to reach the on-call supervisor at [PHONE] (ADM-02, CLN-15).
The trainer reviews the no-smoking rule in client homes (CLN-07) and caregiver safety and workplace violence (CLN-22).

The trainer explains the plan of care: how to read it, that the caregiver does only the tasks listed on it, that changes in condition are reported (CLN-06, CLN-20), and the permitted duties and limits on medication assistance (CLN-13).
The trainer covers professional boundaries, gifts and property (PER-09, CLN-16), documentation of visits, and, for Medicaid clients, timekeeping and EVV (MED-03).
For aides not on the Nurse Aide Registry hired after April 1, 2009, the RN completes and signs the six core-skill verification before assignment (see PER-02).
The employee takes a short quiz or return-demonstration review. The trainer corrects gaps and repeats the missed content.

The trainer and the employee sign and date the Orientation Completion Record, which lists each topic, date, length, trainer and the signatures. The Service Supervisor files it in the personnel record within 5 business days (PER-03).
Orientation hours are paid time under PER-08. The Agency Director reviews orientation completion for each new hire at the 30-day mark.

responsibilities.duty: Implements the Bill of Rights and ensures orientation includes it; approves the orientation content.
Schedules orientation, confirms completion before assignment and files records.
Teaches clinical, infection control and plan of care content and verifies core skills.
Attends all of orientation, asks questions and signs the completion record.
